Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectable upfront  
- Both liver metastases are ≤3 cm, located in separate peripheral segments (II and V) amenable to limited anatomical resections (segmentectomy or wedge) with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on imaging.  
- The primary left‑sided colon tumor is resectable by standard left hemicolectomy.  
- The patient has no significant comorbidities that would preclude major abdominal surgery.  
→ The disease meets criteria for immediate curative‑intent surgery; therefore it is classified as “Resectable upfront”.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Urgent management of the symptomatic primary: Perform a left hemicolectomy (open or laparoscopic) to relieve the sub‑occlusive syndrome; intra‑operative assessment of peritoneal surfaces and regional nodes.  
- Pathology review: Determine T‑stage, nodal status, and margin status; confirm R0 resection of the colon.  
- Systemic therapy: Because of high‑risk features (large primary, CEA 120 ng/mL, synchronous liver mets), initiate postoperative systemic chemotherapy. Preferred regimen: FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given RAS wild‑type status. Plan 3 months (8‑9 cycles) before liver surgery.  
- Restaging after chemotherapy: Repeat contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest to confirm that the metastases remain resectable and to exclude new extra‑hepatic lesions.  
- Curative liver surgery: Proceed to anatomical segmentectomy of segment II and segment V (or combined wedge resections) aiming for R0 margins, using intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate lesion boundaries and vascular anatomy. Ensure a future liver remnant >30 % of total liver volume; consider portal vein embolization only if volumetry is borderline.  
- Post‑hepatectomy management: Complete the planned 6‑month total duration of systemic therapy (additional 3 months after liver resection) and consider adjuvant oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy if pathology shows high‑risk features (e.g., >3 cm total tumor burden, nodal positivity).  
- Surveillance: CEA monitoring every 3 months and imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelets) and assessment of hepatic reserve.  
- Volumetric analysis of future liver remnant to confirm adequacy.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and cardiopulmonary evaluation to gauge operative risk.  
- Detailed description of the obstruction (duration, need for decompression) to determine urgency of colon resection.  
- BRAF mutation status and any other molecular markers that could influence systemic therapy choice.  
- Precise relationship of liver lesions to major vascular structures (portal/hepatic veins) on imaging.  
- Patient’s preference regarding staged versus simultaneous resections.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases (segments II and V, 2.2 cm and 3 cm), bilobar but peripheral, without radiologic evidence of extrahepatic disease. Both lesions appear technically amenable to limited parenchymal-sparing resections (wedge/segmentectomy) with preservation of adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: management of the symptomatic primary tumor
• The subocclusive presentation makes the left colonic lesion the immediate priority.
• Perform an oncologic left colectomy first (or ileostomy) with lymphadenectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) to treat the obstruction risk and allow safe continuation of the oncologic strategy.
• Alternative : consider a temporary diversion before colectomy according to exact degree of subocclusion.

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery from colectomy
• After the emergent procedure, perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise 
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), the situation suggests biologically active disease; short-course neoadjuvant therapy allows treatment of micrometastases and assessment of tumor biology.
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT decision and tolerance.

C. Liver surgery after restaging (liver-first not indicated here due to symptoms)
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and CT restaging.
• If stability or response is observed, proceed to parenchymal-sparing liver resections: segment II wedge/segmentectomy and segment V wedge/segmentectomy guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 margins (>1mm) while preserving maximal liver parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Post-hepatectomy therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including pre-operative cycles).
• Close postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially high tumor marker level.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact degree of subocclusion and whether an temporary diversion is required before colectomy.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of both metastases to confirm feasibility of parenchymal-sparing resections.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Exact location of the left colon tumor (descending vs sigmoid) influencing surgical planning.
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Perform liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectable upfront  
- The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral liver metastasis in segment VI amenable to wedge resection or segmentectomy with adequate future liver remnant.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on FDG‑PET.  
- The primary ileocecal tumor is resectable by standard right hemicolectomy.  
- No functional, anatomical, or oncologic contraindications are reported.  
→ Therefore the disease is classified as “Resectable upfront”.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative work‑up:  
  • Verify performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and cardiopulmonary fitness.  
  • Obtain liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, albumin, and calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume; a FLR > 30 % in a normal liver is sufficient.  
  • Review colonoscopy and pathology to confirm T‑stage and nodal status.  
- Surgical plan (simultaneous resection):  
  • Perform a right hemicolectomy (or ileocecal resection) with oncologic lymphadenectomy aiming for R0 margins.  
  • Conduct a parenchymal‑sparing liver resection of the segment VI lesion (wedge resection or segmentectomy) with a 1‑cm margin, using intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude additional occult metastases.  
  • Ensure hemostasis and consider low‑central venous pressure anesthesia to minimize blood loss.  
- Post‑operative management:  
  • Pathology review of both specimens; if margins are negative and nodal status is favorable, proceed to adjuvant systemic therapy.  
  • Recommended adjuvant chemotherapy: 6 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX), given KRAS mutation excludes anti‑EGFR agents; consider adding bevacizumab only if high‑risk features are present.  
  • Initiate surveillance: CEA every 3‑6 months, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen annually for the first 3 years, colonoscopy at 1 year.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- No essential data are lacking to make a definitive resectability and management recommendation.  
(If any of the following were unknown, they would be required: performance status, liver function tests, FLR volumetry, detailed T‑stage and nodal involvement of the primary tumor, and comorbidities that could affect surgical risk.)
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
The liver lesion (1.8 cm in segment III) is technically resectable with a limited parenchymal resection, and the rectal primary is amenable to curative resection. However, definitive rectal surgery requires a pre‑operative short‑course radiotherapy (or chemoradiotherapy) as a mandatory step before resection. This prerequisite intervention makes the case “potentially resectable” rather than “resectable upfront”.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Short‑course radiotherapy for the rectal tumor (5 × 5 Gy over 1 week).  
• During the interval after radiotherapy (≈6–8 weeks), initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to address micrometastatic disease and confirm biologic behavior of the metastasis.  
• Restaging with pelvic MRI and liver MRI/CT after chemotherapy to verify that the liver lesion remains resectable and that there is no new extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Surgical phase (options, choose based on intra‑operative assessment and patient fitness):  
   – Simultaneous approach: low anterior resection (total mesorectal excision) combined with a non‑anatomical wedge or segmentectomy of segment III, performed in the same operation.  
   – Staged approach (if operative risk or liver concerns): first complete rectal resection (after radiotherapy), allow recovery, then perform liver resection 4–6 weeks later.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (additional 3–6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) to complete a standard peri‑operative systemic regimen.  
• Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) every 6 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Baseline liver function tests and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
• Comprehensive performance status (ECOG/ASA) and cardiopulmonary evaluation given smoking history.  
• Detailed mesorectal fascia status and distance of tumor from the anal verge on MRI.  
• BRAF mutation status and microsatellite instability (MSI) status of the tumor.  
• Exact number of positive lymph nodes and extracapsular spread on pathology (if already resected).  
• Patient’s preference regarding simultaneous versus staged surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
B. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT . Chest CT.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Detailed relationship of the liver lesion to segment III vascular structures on liver MRI.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Three liver lesions are ≤3 cm, located in segments IV, V and VI with only partial contact to the right portal branch and no radiologic invasion, allowing limited anatomical or non‑anatomical resections.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is reported; the primary transverse colon tumor is amenable to standard colectomy.  
- Assuming adequate future liver remnant (>30 % in a 72‑year‑old) and acceptable performance status, both the hepatic and colonic components can be removed safely in a single operative session.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative work‑up:  
  • Full liver function panel, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan to confirm hepatic reserve.  
  • Volumetric CT or MRI to calculate future liver remnant; if <30 % consider portal vein embolisation (PVE).  
  • Assessment of cardiopulmonary fitness (e.g., ECOG, cardiology clearance).  
- Surgical plan (simultaneous resection preferred):  
  1. Mid‑line or extended right colectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy for the transverse colon primary, aiming for R0 margins.  
  2. Limited liver resection: segmentectomy of segment IV and non‑anatomical wedge resections of lesions in segments V and VI, preserving portal inflow and biliary drainage; intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins and portal anatomy.  
  3. Achieve negative margins (≥1 cm when feasible) and preserve ≥30 % functional liver parenchyma.  
- Post‑operative systemic therapy:  
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy for 6 months (CAPOX or FOLFOX) given KRAS‑mutated, BRAF‑wild type disease; anti‑EGFR agents are not indicated.  
  • Monitor CEA and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.  
- If intra‑operative findings reveal insufficient liver remnant or unexpected vascular invasion, convert to staged approach: first colectomy, then reassess liver resectability after recovery, possibly employing PVE or two‑stage hepatectomy.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal).  
- Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance).  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume calculation.  
- Exact location and length of colon tumor relative to vascular structures to confirm feasibility of R0 colectomy.  
- Presence or absence of additional extra‑hepatic metastases (e.g., lung, peritoneum).  
- Baseline nutritional status and frailty assessment.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of right hepatectomy.F. Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
Reasoning: The four liver metastases are small (≤2.9 cm), peripherally located in segments II, III, V and VIII, and there is no involvement of major hepatic vessels or extra‑hepatic disease. Assuming a normal liver background, resection of the left lateral sector (II‑III) together with limited segmental or wedge resections of V and VIII would leave an adequate future liver remnant (>30 % of total liver volume). The primary sigmoid lesion is resectable with a standard oncologic colectomy. No anatomical or oncologic contraindications to immediate surgery are evident.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   • Obtain liver volumetry (CT‑based) to confirm FLR adequacy.  
   • Perform baseline liver function tests, coagulation profile, and cardiopulmonary assessment (ASA, ECOG).  
   • Discuss with anesthesia and radiology for intra‑operative ultrasound planning.  

2. Surgical plan – simultaneous resection (preferred)  
   • Laparoscopic or open sigmoid colectomy with oncologic margins and adequate lymphadenectomy (D3).  
   • Hepatic phase: intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion locations; perform left lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) and parenchymal‑sparing resections of lesions in segments V and VIII (segmentectomy or wedge resection) aiming for R0 margins.  
   • Use Pringle maneuver only if needed; employ low‑central venous pressure anesthesia to minimize blood loss.  

3. Post‑operative oncologic management  
   • Pathology review for margin status, number of positive nodes, and KRAS/NRAS status (already wild‑type).  
   • Initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy within 6‑8 weeks (6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX).  
   • Given RAS wild‑type and high pre‑operative CEA, consider adding anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) to adjuvant regimen in a clinical‑trial setting or if high‑risk features persist.  
   • Schedule CEA monitoring every 3 months and contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative liver volumetry to confirm future liver remnant volume.  
• Baseline liver function (bilirubin, albumin, INR, indocyanine green clearance if available).  
• Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve (ASA/ECOG).  
• Details on planned surgical approach (laparoscopic vs open) and availability of intra‑operative ultrasound.  
These data are essential to finalize operative planning and peri‑operative risk assessment.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of each lesion.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Both hepatic lesions are ≤4 cm, located in segments II and IVa, and the middle hepatic vein is preserved, allowing an anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with an adequate future liver remnant (>30 %).  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is reported on imaging.  
- The primary tumor is technically resectable (right‑sided colon cancer) and there is no indication of obstruction, perforation or bleeding that would preclude a planned operation.  
- Therefore, from an anatomical and functional standpoint, complete (R0) resection of the colon primary and both liver metastases is feasible without the need for portal vein embolization or other preparatory procedures.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Baseline evaluation: obtain full blood count, liver panel, coagulation profile, cardiopulmonary assessment, and calculate the future liver remnant volume (if not already done).  
- Systemic therapy: initiate peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) because the primary is T4N2 and KRAS‑mutated disease carries high recurrence risk. This serves to treat micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology, and may further downsize the liver lesions.  
- Restaging after 2–3 months of chemotherapy with contrast‑enhanced CT and liver MRI. If disease is stable or responding and no new extra‑hepatic sites appear, proceed to surgery.  
- Surgical plan (choose based on patient fitness and intra‑operative considerations):  
   • Simultaneous resection: right hemicolectomy with en‑bloc removal of segments II and IVa (or wedge resections) in a single operation, provided operative time and physiologic stress are acceptable.  
   • Staged approach: (a) right hemicolectomy first, recover 4–6 weeks, then liver resection; or (b) liver‑first resection if the primary is asymptomatic and liver disease is deemed the limiting factor.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (continue or switch to a postoperative regimen) to consolidate the response.  
- Surveillance: serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal).  
- Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine‑green clearance or other quantitative assessment of hepatic reserve.  
- Precise future liver remnant volume calculation.  
- Presence or absence of symptoms from the primary tumor (obstruction, bleeding, perforation).  
- Detailed staging of regional lymph nodes (number of positive nodes, extracapsular spread).  
- Patient’s preferences regarding simultaneous versus staged surgery.  
- Any prior neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy already administered.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases located in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. MRI confirms preservation of the middle hepatic vein and no major vascular invasion. Both lesions are technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections (in case of effective tumor shrinkage with neoadjuvant therapy) or left hepatectomy with preservation of the middle hepatic vein. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and favorable anatomical location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: control of the primary tumor
• The elevated CEA level (95 ng/mL) and right-sided T4N2 colon cancer represents locally advanced disease and is the immediate oncologic priority.
• Given the high CEA level (95 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Assess potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel, duodenum)
• 3 options
-	Perform an oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis, first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications.
-	Perform an derivation ileostomy first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications during chemotherapy.
-	Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).

• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period allows treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Liver surgery after restaging
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan restaging.
• If tumor response is observed on primary cancer : proceed to oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis
• If tumor response is observed on liver metastases, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment II wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment IVa wedge/segmentectomy.
• If stability or progression is observed, proceed to anatomic left hepatectomy preserving the middle hepatic vein guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information

Case_Content:
Man, 47 years old,at the abdominal CT scan T3N0 upper rectal cancer with three liver metastases (segments VI, VII and VIII), sizes 1-2 cm. CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. No other lesions on PET.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases primarily resectable, considered for combined treatment after short-course pelvic radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectable upfront  
The three liver metastases are small (1‑2 cm), confined to segments VI‑VIII of the right liver, and there is no evidence of extra‑hepatic disease on PET. A parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy can remove all lesions while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. The primary rectal tumor is T3N0 and amenable to curative resection after short‑course pelvic radiotherapy. No oncologic or anatomic contraindications are present; therefore the disease is resectable without prerequisite down‑staging.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) as already planned.  
2. Restaging CT/MRI 1–2 weeks after radiotherapy to confirm unchanged liver disease and assess postoperative liver volume.  
3. Proceed to combined curative surgery within 1–2 weeks of radiotherapy:  
   • Total mesorectal excision (low anterior resection) with negative circumferential margin.  
   • Parenchymal‑sparing liver resection using intra‑operative ultrasound to guide segmental or wedge resections of lesions in segments VI, VII and VIII, aiming for ≥5 mm margin.  
   • Ensure intra‑operative assessment of liver inflow/outflow and FLR; no portal vein embolization required.  
4. Post‑operative recovery and early mobilization; discharge when criteria met (usually POD 5‑7).  
5. Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS‑wild type) initiated after wound healing (≈4‑6 weeks post‑op).  
6. Surveillance: CEA every 3 months for 2 years, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen every 6 months, colonoscopy at 1 year.

If intra‑operative findings reveal insufficient liver remnant or unexpected disease burden, convert to a staged approach (liver first, then rectal resection after recovery) and consider portal vein embolization if needed.

Step 3 - Missing data  
No essential data are lacking for a reliable resection and treatment plan. Relevant information such as performance status, liver function tests, volumetric assessment of future liver remnant, and BRAF status are desirable but not mandatory to proceed with the outlined strategy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three small liver metastases (1–2 cm) located in segments VI, VII, and VIII, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Although confined to the right liver, the lesions seem technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution pelvic MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm primary tumor location, circumferential and distal margins, lymph nodes involvement, invasion of fascia recti. A chest CT scan for extrahepatic disease.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and pelvic MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both primary tumor and liver metastases

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N0 upper rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the three lesions using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segments VI, VII and VIII metastases with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segments VI, VII and VIII metastases followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the segments VI, VII and VIII metastases, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A.	Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, and circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI influencing surgical approach and anastomotic risk
B.	A chest CT scan for extrahepatic disease
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three liver lesions on MRI.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of hypertension, discovery of left colon cancer and a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 40 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, anatomically favorable for a single resection.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Single 2.7 cm metastasis in segment IVb is anatomically amenable to a limited hepatic resection with an adequate future liver remnant.  
- No evidence of extra‑hepatic disease on the provided CT.  
- Patient’s comorbidity (controlled hypertension) does not preclude major abdominal surgery.  
- Therefore curative resection can be planned without the need for down‑staging therapy or additional information.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Confirm complete staging: colonoscopy with biopsy, full thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic imaging (CT or MRI), baseline liver function tests, and assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1).  
- Obtain RAS mutational status (KRAS/NRAS) to guide use of anti‑EGFR agents in the adjuvant setting.  
- Proceed with a simultaneous curative operation:  
   • Left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
   • Anatomical segment IVb resection or wedge excision with negative margins (≥1 cm) and intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm no additional lesions.  
- Pathology review of both specimens to verify R0 resection and assess tumor grade, lymphovascular invasion, and nodal status.  
- Post‑operative systemic therapy: 6 months of adjuvant FOLFOX (or CAPOX) is recommended for stage IV disease after R0 resection.  
   • If RAS wild‑type, add anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) to the regimen, given left‑sided primary.  
- Follow‑up surveillance: CEA every 3 months for 2 years, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- RAS (KRAS/NRAS) mutational status.  
- Detailed liver function tests and volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant.  
- Cardiopulmonary fitness (e.g., VO₂ max, echocardiogram) to confirm operative tolerance in a 70‑year‑old.  
- Confirmation that chest imaging excludes pulmonary metastases.  
These data would solidify peri‑operative risk assessment but are not essential to classify the case as resectable upfront.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis located in segment IVb, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesion is anatomically favorable for a a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary metastasis with favorable anatomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm the relationship of the lesion to segment IVb vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology, however the KRAS status is unknown.
• BRAF wild-type and MSS status do not modify the surgical indication.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT. 

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment IVb wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : simultaneous left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures (Wisneski et al.; Kim et al.) However, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. K-Ras status, grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor with two contiguous liver metastases in segment VI (2.1 and 2.4 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 180 ng/mL, KRAS mutation.
MDT Discussion: Limited and accessible liver involvement, no indication for upfront chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
Reasoning: The patient has a solitary primary sigmoid lesion (T3N1) amenable to standard oncologic colectomy and two small (<3 cm) contiguous liver metastases confined to segment VI. There is no radiologic evidence of vascular invasion, biliary involvement, or extra‑hepatic disease. The lesions are anatomically accessible, allowing a limited hepatic resection (segmentectomy or wedge) with an expected future liver remnant >30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver. KRAS mutation and elevated CEA do not contraindicate surgery. Therefore, curative resection can be performed without prerequisite systemic therapy.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   • Complete colonoscopic assessment of the primary tumor and obtain biopsies if not already done.  
   • Multiphasic liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to confirm number, size, and exact location of hepatic lesions and to assess vascular anatomy.  
   • Chest CT to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   • Baseline liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance or volumetric CT to verify adequate future liver remnant.  
   • Assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and comorbidities.  

2. Surgical plan – one‑stage simultaneous resection  
   • Laparoscopic or open sigmoid colectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy (D3) respecting mesocolic plane.  
   • Concurrent hepatic resection: segment VI anatomical resection (or non‑anatomic wedge) encompassing both metastases with negative margins (R0). Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries and rule out additional occult disease.  

3. Post‑operative oncologic management  
   • Recovery and wound assessment; aim for discharge by postoperative day 5‑7 if uncomplicated.  
   • Initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) within 6‑8 weeks, given node‑positive primary (N1) and high pre‑operative CEA, to address micrometastatic risk.  
   • Consider adding anti‑EGFR therapy only if RAS wild‑type; in this case KRAS mutant, so continue standard cytotoxic regimen.  

4. Surveillance  
   • CEA measurement every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
   • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest, abdomen, pelvis at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Quantitative liver functional reserve (e.g., ICG‑R15, volumetric FLR calculation).  
- Chest imaging results to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Exact location of the primary lesion relative to mesenteric vessels (to plan extent of colectomy).  
These pieces of information are essential to confirm surgical safety and to finalize the operative approach.

Woman, 65 years old, simultaneous discovery of a right colon adenocarcinoma and a 3 cm liver metastasis in segment VII at the abdominal CT scan CEA 70 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Deep but resectable metastasis, discussion of simultaneous versus sequential surgery.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront: The liver lesion is solitary, 3 cm, located in segment VII, and described as “deep but resectable.” A right hemicolectomy for the primary tumor is also technically feasible. Assuming adequate future liver remnant and no extra‑hepatic disease, both lesions can be removed in a single operative session without the need for down‑staging therapy or additional information.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Confirm full staging: contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver, chest CT, and colonoscopy to verify absence of extra‑hepatic disease and to define T/N stage of the colon primary.  
- Multidisciplinary planning: schedule simultaneous resection if the patient’s performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and cardiopulmonary reserve are acceptable.  
- Operative plan:  
   • Right hemicolectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy (D3) for the colon primary.  
   • Anatomical segment VII resection (segmentectomy) or wedge resection with negative margins, guided by intra‑operative ultrasound.  
   • Ensure a future liver remnant >30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver; no portal vein embolization required.  
- Post‑operative management:  
   • Pathology review for margin status, nodal involvement, and tumor grade.  
   • Initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6‑12 cycles of FOLFOX).  
   • Because the tumor is RAS wild‑type, consider adding anti‑EGFR therapy (cetuximab or panitumumab) in the adjuvant setting if high‑risk features are present (e.g., T4, N2, poorly differentiated).  
   • Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
No critical data are lacking to make a definitive resectability judgment or to outline a surgical plan. Essential information that would further refine the recommendation (but is not currently prohibitive) includes: ECOG performance status, detailed liver function tests, volumetric assessment of future liver remnant, exact T/N stage of the colon cancer, presence/absence of regional nodal disease, and BRAF mutation status.

MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, left liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
The three hepatic lesions are confined to the left hepatic lobe, are ≤2.5 cm, and no extra‑hepatic disease is reported. A left hepatectomy (or left lateral segmentectomy) would leave an adequate future liver remnant (right lobe) in a 53‑year‑old with presumably normal liver function. The primary sigmoid lesion is T3N0 and technically amenable to standard oncologic resection. No vascular invasion, biliary obstruction, or functional contraindication is described, therefore the disease is technically resectable without prerequisite down‑staging.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   • Full liver function panel, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan if steatosis suspected.  
   • Volumetric CT or MRI to confirm that the future liver remnant will be ≥30 % of total liver volume.  
   • Baseline chest CT (already performed) and PET‑CT if any doubt about occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   • Assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and comorbidities.  

2. Systemic therapy (optional but recommended)  
   • Because the disease is synchronous and the patient has a high CEA and KRAS‑mutated tumor, give 2–3 cycles of oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) to test tumor biology and treat micrometastatic disease.  
   • Re‑image after chemotherapy to confirm that all lesions remain resectable and no new sites have appeared.

   • If post‑chemotherapy imaging confirms resectability, proceed with a one‑stage operation:

   • If intra‑operative findings reveal unexpected disease (e.g., extensive bilobar involvement), convert to staged approach or abort hepatic resection.  

4. Post‑operative management  
   • Resume systemic chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative therapy (including the pre‑operative cycles).  
   • Monitor CEA and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.

• Quantitative liver function assessment and future liver remnant volumetry.  
• Patient’s performance status and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
• Detailed anatomic relationship of the liver lesions to major vessels/ducts (to confirm feasibility of a safe margin).  
• Presence or absence of microscopic nodal involvement in the primary (pathology after resection).  
• Baseline PET‑CT or additional staging to definitively exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.

Case_Content:
Woman, 66 years old, high rectal T3N1 cancer with a single 1.5 cm metastasis in segment II at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 50 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Peripheral resectable metastasis, possibility of combined surgery after pelvic treatment.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The solitary 1.5 cm lesion in segment II is anatomically resectable with a peripheral wedge or segmentectomy and would leave an adequate future liver remnant.  
- The primary rectal tumor is T3N1 and located high in the rectum, which according to current rectal cancer guidelines requires neoadjuvant pelvic chemoradiotherapy before definitive surgery.  
- Completion of this neoadjuvant treatment is a prerequisite for any curative‑intent resection of the primary, therefore the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.”  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate long‑course neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the rectal primary (50.4 Gy in 28 fractions with concurrent capecitabine or 5‑FU).  
- Concurrently deliver systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX or CAPOX) to address micrometastatic disease and to begin treatment of the liver metastasis.  
- Restage 6–8 weeks after completion of chemoradiotherapy with high‑resolution pelvic MRI and liver MRI/contrast‑enhanced CT to confirm tumor response and unchanged liver lesion size/position.  
- If the rectal tumor has down‑staged to a resectable stage (≤T3a, no threatening mesorectal fascia) and the liver lesion remains peripheral and resectable, proceed to a combined operation: low anterior resection (or appropriate sphincter‑preserving resection) together with a segment II wedge/segmentectomy, performed by a colorectal and hepatobiliary team in the same session.  
- If intra‑operative assessment suggests that a simultaneous liver resection would compromise hepatic reserve or increase morbidity, adopt a staged approach: first the rectal resection, followed by liver resection within 6–8 weeks, provided the patient recovers adequately.  
- Complete total peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy to a cumulative 6 months (including neoadjuvant cycles) as adjuvant therapy, given the node‑positive primary.  
- Ongoing surveillance with CEA, colonoscopy, and periodic liver imaging per standard guidelines.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve).

Man, 58 years old, left T4aN2 colon cancer, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Max size 3.8 cm. CEA 330 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.

Potentially resectable: The three hepatic lesions (segments IV, V, VIII) can be cleared surgically, but definitive feasibility depends on (a) quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve, and (b) confirmation that there are no occult extra‑hepatic sites (e.g., pulmonary or peritoneal disease). Without these data we cannot guarantee that an upfront major hepatectomy would leave an adequate FLR or that the disease is truly limited to the liver.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) to treat micrometastatic disease, assess tumor biology, and potentially downsize liver lesions.

• If FLR is <30 % in a normal liver (or <40 % in a steatotic/chemotherapy‑injured liver), schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left lateral segments (II‑III) and segment I.  
• Re‑image 2–4 weeks after PVE to confirm adequate FLR hypertrophy.  
• Surgical plan:  
   – If FLR is sufficient after PVE (or was adequate initially), proceed with an extended right hepatectomy (segments V, VI, VII, VIII plus segment IVb) aiming for R0 margins.

• Follow‑up: CEA monitoring every 3 months, imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

• Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT, PET‑CT, diagnostic laparoscopy).  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary, hepatic steatosis, prior chemotherapy‑induced liver injury).  
• Details on the primary tumor’s symptomatology (obstruction, bleeding) that might dictate priority of resection.  
• Baseline liver imaging to assess tumor proximity to major vascular/biliary structures.

Response:

- The liver lesion is solitary (2.8 cm), located in segment V, a peripheral site amenable to wedge resection or segmentectomy with an expected adequate future liver remnant.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is reported on staging CT.  
- The primary rectal tumor is T2N0, indicating early stage without nodal involvement; thus it is technically resectable with total mesorectal excision.  
- The patient is 49 years old, presumably with good performance status, and there are no reported contraindications (e.g., severe liver dysfunction, portal hypertension).  
- Consequently, both the hepatic and rectal components meet standard anatomical and oncologic criteria for immediate surgical resection; no prerequisite therapy or missing critical information is identified that would preclude upfront surgery.  

Classification: Resectable upfront  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Stage 1: Multidisciplinary planning – Confirm resectability with liver volumetry (CT volumetry or MRI) and obtain high‑resolution pelvic MRI to define the rectal tumor’s distance from the anal verge and circumferential resection margin (CRM).  
- Stage 2: Primary‑first approach  
   • If the rectal tumor is located >5 cm from the anal verge and MRI shows a clear CRM, proceed directly to total mesorectal excision (TME) without neoadjuvant radiotherapy.  
   • If the tumor is low (<5 cm) or MRI suggests a threatened CRM, give short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) or long‑course chemoradiation (45–50 Gy with concurrent fluoropyrimidine) before TME.  
- Stage 3: Peri‑operative systemic therapy – Because KRAS is mutated, anti‑EGFR agents are not indicated. Offer peri‑operative FOLFOX (or CAPOX) chemotherapy:  
   • Administer 2–3 cycles pre‑operatively (optional) to address micrometastatic disease and confirm liver lesion stability.  
   • Resume postoperative chemotherapy for a total of 6 months (including any pre‑operative cycles).  
- Stage 4: Hepatic resection – After recovery from rectal surgery (typically 4–6 weeks), perform a limited anatomical resection of segment V (segmentectomy or wedge) with negative margins, using intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and assess for additional occult disease.  
- Stage 5: Surveillance – Serial CEA measurements every 3 months for the first 2 years, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis every 6 months, and colonoscopy at 1 year post‑resection.  

Alternative option (if the patient is highly fit and the rectal tumor is amenable to low‑morbidity resection): simultaneous TME and liver segmentectomy in a single operative session, performed by a coordinated colorectal‑hepatic team to reduce overall treatment time.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge and MRI assessment of circumferential resection margin.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR) and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Full staging imaging of the chest (CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Results of colonoscopy (extent of luminal disease, need for endoscopic stenting).  
- Details of any prior neoadjuvant therapy already administered.  

These data are required to finalize the operative plan and confirm that the “resectable upfront” classification remains appropriate.

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven bilobar liver metastases, sizes 1 to 4 cm at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 520 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: vascular contact with the right portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Metastases not resectable upfront, considered for conversion chemotherapy FOLFOX + bevacizumab.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: Current imaging shows seven bilobar metastases (1‑4 cm) with vascular contact to the right portal branch, which precludes safe upfront liver resection. Down‑staging with conversion chemotherapy is required to achieve a resectable disease burden and to clarify the relationship of the lesions to critical vasculature. The need for this specific pre‑operative intervention meets the definition of “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy with FOLFOX plus bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
- Administer 2–3 months of therapy, then obtain repeat contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and CT to assess tumor response, lesion size, and vascular involvement.  
- Monitor CEA trend and assess for radiologic response (RECIST) and potential conversion to ≤4 lesions amenable to a single‑stage resection or to a two‑stage approach.  
- If response is adequate and future liver remnant (FLR) volume is ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in steatotic liver), plan surgical sequence:  
   • Perform right hemicolectomy (or segmental resection) of the primary tumor either before or simultaneously with liver surgery, depending on symptomatology and operative risk.  
   • For bilobar disease, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy: first stage – clearance of lesions in the future liver remnant (e.g., left lateral section) plus portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branch to hypertrophy the FLR; second stage – right hepatectomy after adequate hypertrophy (typically 4–6 weeks).  
   • If post‑chemotherapy imaging shows all lesions confined to one hemi‑liver with adequate FLR, proceed with a single‑stage anatomical or non‑anatomical resection.  
- Observe a minimum 6‑week interval after the last bevacizumab dose before any major surgery to reduce wound‑healing complications.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (continuation of FOLFOX or switch to CAPOX) for a total of 6 months of systemic therapy, adjusted to pathologic response and margin status.  
- Continue regular surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, albumin, INR) and quantitative liver function assessment (e.g., ICG clearance).  
- Volumetric analysis of the future liver remnant to determine need for portal vein embolization.  
- Detailed anatomical mapping of each metastasis relative to hepatic veins, portal branches, and biliary ducts.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that may affect chemotherapy tolerance or surgical risk.  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (symptomatic obstruction, perforation, prior resection).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease beyond the liver (e.g., lung, peritoneum).  
- Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive multimodal therapy.

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: The current imaging shows four bilobar metastases, one abutting the right hepatic vein, making an immediate R0 liver resection unlikely without downsizing. The MDT plan to repeat imaging after 4 cycles of chemotherapy indicates that a prerequisite systemic treatment response is required before a definitive surgical decision can be made.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate conversion systemic therapy:  
  • Preferred regimen for a left‑sided, RAS‑wild‑type tumor – FOLFOX (or FOLFIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab).  
  • Consider adding bevacizumab only if anti‑EGFR is contraindicated or response is suboptimal.  
- Administer 4–6 cycles, monitor tolerance, and reassess CEA trend.  
- Restaging after chemotherapy:  
  • Multiphasic contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) with volumetric analysis to determine residual tumor size, relationship to hepatic veins/portal structures, and future liver remnant (FLR) volume.  
  • Colonoscopy or high‑resolution CT of the abdomen/pelvis to confirm no new extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Decision algorithm based on restaging:  
  • If all lesions shrink to ≤3 cm and a clear margin (>1 cm) can be achieved with an FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % if steatosis/cirrhosis), proceed to simultaneous sigmoid colectomy and single‑stage liver resection (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing as appropriate).  
  • If lesions remain bilobar but resectable only after major hepatectomy with insufficient FLR, plan a two‑stage approach:  
    – Stage 1: Portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments to be resected, plus sigmoid resection if not already performed.  
    – Re‑image after 2–3 weeks to confirm FLR hypertrophy; if adequate, proceed to Stage 2 liver resection (right or left hepatectomy, or extended resection) aiming for R0 margins.  
  • If disease remains unresectable after maximal chemotherapy or FLR cannot be achieved, consider locoregional therapies (radiofrequency ablation, microwave ablation, or stereotactic body radiotherapy) for residual lesions and continue systemic therapy.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6‑month total duration) after recovery, with consideration of maintenance biologic if disease‑free.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Baseline performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and assessment for steatosis or fibrosis.  
- Precise size of each hepatic lesion and distance to major vascular structures (right hepatic vein, portal pedicles).  
- Volumetric measurement of future liver remnant.  
- BRAF mutation status (to refine systemic therapy).  
- Status of the primary sigmoid tumor (obstructive, perforated) and whether it has been resected or requires urgent surgery.  
- Presence or absence of other extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum).

Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: Current imaging shows six bilobar metastases (2‑5 cm) with involvement of the middle hepatic vein, making an upfront liver‑first or simultaneous resection unsafe because the future liver remnant would be insufficient and vascular reconstruction would be required. • Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy aimed at maximal tumor shrinkage and potential conversion to resectability. Preferred regimen: FOLFOXIRI (or FOLFOX/FOLFIRI) combined with bevacizumab, 6–8 cycles, with close radiologic assessment after 2–3 cycles.

Man, 68 years old, right T4aN2 colon cancer, ten bilobar liver metastases (1-4 cm) at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 1350 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type. Liver MRI: contact with IVC and left portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, induction therapy planned before re-evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
- Category: Potentially resectable  
- Reasoning: The presence of ten bilobar metastases, some abutting the IVC and left portal branch, makes an immediate R0 liver resection technically infeasible. The MDT has already planned induction systemic therapy, indicating that tumor downsizing or conversion is required before a definitive surgical assessment can be made. Therefore a prerequisite (effective neoadjuvant chemotherapy) must be completed prior to declaring the disease resectable.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy: preferred regimen FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab for 3–4 months (6–8 cycles), assuming adequate performance status and organ function.  
- If KRAS/NRAS wild‑type (information pending), consider adding anti‑EGFR (cetuximab or panitumumab) to the regimen for increased response rates.  
- Monitor response with serial CEA levels and repeat contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) after 2–3 months of therapy.  
- Re‑evaluate resectability after imaging:  
   • If ≥70 % of lesions regress to ≤3 cm and no new extra‑hepatic disease appears, calculate future liver remnant (FLR).  
   • If FLR <30 % of total liver volume, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments to be resected, allowing hypertrophy over 2–4 weeks.  
- Surgical plan (once adequate down‑staging achieved):  
   • Stage 1: Resection of the primary right colon tumor (right hemicolectomy) – can be performed either before or concurrently with liver surgery depending on patient condition and intra‑operative logistics.  
   • Stage 2: Liver resection – likely a two‑stage hepatectomy or a single extended hepatectomy after PVE, using intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate margins. Aim for R0 resection of all visible disease; consider parenchymal‑sparing techniques (segmentectomy, wedge resections) to preserve liver function.  
   • If after conversion therapy only a limited number of lesions remain amenable to a single operation, a simultaneous colon and liver resection may be performed.  
- Post‑operative management: resume adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 6 months total peri‑operative chemotherapy) and consider targeted agents based on final molecular profile.  
- Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years.

- KRAS, NRAS, and MSI status (to guide use of anti‑EGFR or immunotherapy).  
- Baseline liver function tests and quantitative FLR assessment (CT volumetry).  
- Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities influencing chemotherapy tolerance and surgical risk.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease beyond the liver (e.g., lung, peritoneum).  
- Details of vascular involvement (degree of IVC/portal contact) to assess need for vascular reconstruction.  
- Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive multimodal therapy.

Case_Content:
Woman, 50 years old, T3N1M1 rectal cancer, five liver metastases (segments II, III, IVa, VI, VII), max size 4.1 cm. CEA 370 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Extensive bilobar involvement, possibility of conversion depending on response to chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has five bilobar liver metastases up to 4.1 cm, which can be resected only if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved and if the lesions can be cleared with negative margins. Critical information required to confirm feasibility—quantitative liver volumetry, FLR percentage, and functional liver reserve (e.g., ICG clearance)—is not provided. Without these data, a definitive upfront resection cannot be planned, but the disease is not automatically unresectable; it may become resectable after downsizing chemotherapy or after portal vein embolization to augment FLR. Hence the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” because the missing FLR assessment is a decisive prerequisite.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain baseline high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and CT volumetry to calculate FLR; assess vascular relationships of each lesion.  
- Perform baseline laboratory work‑up (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG‑R15) and evaluate performance status (ECOG).  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy with an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for 2–3 months aiming for tumor shrinkage and to assess tumor biology.  
- If the rectal primary is symptomatic or at risk for local complications, give short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) or long‑course chemoradiation concurrently with the early cycles of systemic therapy.  
- Re‑image after chemotherapy: repeat MRI/CT and repeat volumetry.  
   • If FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % if underlying liver disease) and all lesions become resectable with clear margins, proceed to liver surgery.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in one lobe, PVE of the contralateral lobe; second stage: resection of the cleared lobe after hypertrophy).  
   • In selected cases with very limited hypertrophy, ALPPS may be contemplated, but only after multidisciplinary consensus.  
- Perform liver resection (anatomic or non‑anatomic as dictated by lesion location) aiming for R0 margins; intra‑operative ultrasound to guide resection.  
- After hepatic surgery and recovery, proceed with definitive rectal surgery (total mesorectal excision) either immediately or after a short interval, depending on patient recovery and oncologic timing.  
- Complete adjuvant systemic therapy (additional 3–6 months) based on pathological response and tolerance.  
- Follow‑up with serial CEA, imaging (CT or MRI every 3–6 months) and colonoscopic surveillance.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative liver volumetry and calculated future liver remnant percentage.  
- Functional liver reserve assessment (ICG‑R15, Child‑Pugh, MELD).  
- Detailed vascular anatomy of each metastasis (proximity to major hepatic veins, portal pedicles).  
- Performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR).  
- Exact distance of rectal tumor from anal verge and involvement of mesorectal fascia.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease beyond the liver (e.g., lung, peritoneum).  
- Patient’s preferences regarding treatment intensity and timing.

• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships.

• Initiate intensive doublet or triplet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) as discussed in MDT.

C. Early radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan every 2 months to assess:

• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:

– Separation from the middle hepatic vein.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections and/or ablation with adequate future liver remnant.

• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
