• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, operated 4 years ago for right colon adenocarcinoma (T3N1M0), no initial recurrence. Surveillance: CEA 180 ng/mL. At the thoraco-abdominal CT scan: two liver lesions segments V and VIII, 2.8 and 3.2 cm. Liver MRI confirms no other foci. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metachronous metastases, anatomically accessible, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Two isolated lesions (2.8 cm in segment V, 3.2 cm in segment VIII) with no extra‑hepatic disease on high‑quality MRI.  
- Anatomical location permits a right hepatectomy or combined segmentectomy V + VIII while preserving an adequate future liver remnant (FLR > 30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver).  
- Patient is 62 y, good performance status, no reported comorbidities that would preclude major hepatic surgery.  
- No vascular invasion or biliary involvement described.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- 1️⃣ Pre‑operative work‑up:  
   • Full liver function panel, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan, and volumetric CT to confirm FLR adequacy.  
   • Cardiopulmonary assessment (e.g., VO₂ max) to verify fitness for major resection.  
- 2️⃣ Surgical plan (performed first because disease is resectable upfront):  
   • Anatomical right hepatectomy or parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy V + VIII aiming for R0 margins (≥1 cm).  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion number and exclude occult disease.  
   • If FLR borderline, consider portal vein embolization pre‑operatively; otherwise proceed directly to resection.  
- 3️⃣ Post‑operative systemic therapy:  
   • Adjuvant chemotherapy for 6 months (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab, given KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
   • Rationale: high pre‑operative CEA (180 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology; adjuvant therapy improves disease‑free survival.  
- 4️⃣ Surveillance:  
   • CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for 3 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile.  
- Quantitative liver function assessment (ICG clearance, mebrofenin uptake) and volumetric measurement of the future liver remnant.  
- Details of any prior systemic therapy or radiotherapy received for the primary tumor.  
- Cardiopulmonary reserve (e.g., VO₂ max, pulmonary function tests).  

These data are needed to confirm surgical safety and to fine‑tune peri‑operative planning, but the available information already supports a recommendation for upfront resection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy.
Reference:

The patient presents with two metachronous liver metastases in segments V and VIII (2.8 and 3.2 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Both lesions are peripherally located in the right liver and technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited, metachronous, anatomically favorable metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Given the high CEA level (180 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.
• Given the metachronous presentation after a long disease-free interval and the limited number of lesions, immediate surgical resection is appropriate without mandatory neoadjuvant chemotherapy cou ld be considered

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, two wedge/segmental resections :
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT.
B. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, operated for low rectal cancer 3 years ago (T3N1M0) after chemoradiotherapy. CEA 95 ng/mL. Liver MRI: lesion in segment II (2.5 cm) and micronodule segment V. RAS wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous metastases, potentially curable, negative extra-hepatic workup.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
The liver disease consists of a solitary 2.5 cm lesion in segment II and a tiny micronodule in segment V. Both lesions are amenable to parenchymal‑sparing resections (segment II wedge or left lateral segmentectomy plus segment V wedge/segmentectomy) with an expected adequate future liver remnant. There is no radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease, the primary rectal cancer has been resected, and the patient’s tumor biology (RAS wild‑type, MSS) does not preclude curative intent. Hence the hepatic disease meets criteria for immediate surgical resection without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• 1. Baseline assessment: obtain performance status (ECOG 0‑1), liver function tests, and volumetric CT to confirm FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if steatosis/cirrhosis).  
• 2. Systemic therapy: initiate peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 3 months FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat occult disease, assess tumor biology, and potentially downsize the micronodule.  
• 3. Restaging after chemotherapy: repeat contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT and CEA. If disease remains limited to the liver with no new lesions, proceed to surgery.  
• 4. Surgical plan:  
   – Perform a parenchymal‑sparing left lateral resection (segment II wedge or formal segment II resection) to achieve R0 margins.  
   – Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate the segment V micronodule; excise with a wedge or limited segmentectomy ensuring ≥ 1 cm margin.  
   – Preserve as much non‑tumorous parenchyma as possible; consider radiofrequency/ microwave ablation for the segment V lesion if intra‑operative margins are questionable.  
• 5. Post‑operative care: monitor liver function, early mobilization, and initiate adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months systemic therapy (including pre‑operative courses).  
• 6. Surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, liver MRI/CT every 6 months, and colonoscopic surveillance per guidelines.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Current performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky).  
• Detailed liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and any underlying liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis).  
• Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
• Exact size and relationship of the segment V micronodule to major vessels/ducts.  
• Prior systemic therapy exposure and tolerance.  
• Comorbidities that could affect peri‑operative risk (cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal).  

These data would refine the peri‑operative plan but are not essential to conclude that the patient is a candidate for upfront curative liver resection.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of left colectomy for T4N2 tumor, in remission for 2 years. Surveillance: CEA 430 ng/mL. FDG-PET: three bilobar liver lesions, 2-3 cm, no other foci. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous liver recurrence, potentially resectable after discussion.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has three bilobar liver metastases (2‑3 cm each) with no extra‑hepatic disease, which in principle can be removed surgically. However, definitive resectability hinges on (a) quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve, and (b) the relationship of the lesions to major vascular structures. Without liver volumetry, portal venous pressure data, and detailed segmental anatomy, we cannot confirm that an adequate FLR can be achieved with a single operation; therefore a prerequisite step (pre‑operative volumetric/functional assessment, possibly portal vein embolization) is required before definitive surgery.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- 1. Obtain high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT with 3‑D reconstruction to define lesion location, vascular involvement, and calculate FLR volume.  
- 2. Perform liver function testing (ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh, MELD) and assess performance status (ECOG).  
- 3. Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to assess tumor biology, potentially downsize lesions, and treat micrometastatic disease.

   • Option A – Single‑stage, parenchyma‑sparing hepatectomy (e.g., combined right posterior sectorectomy + left lateral segmentectomy) using intra‑operative ultrasound to achieve R0 margins while preserving maximal liver tissue.  
   • Option B – Two‑stage hepatectomy if lesions are widely separated: first stage resect lesions in one lobe (or perform PVE), second stage resect contralateral lobe after hypertrophy.  
- 6. Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., continuation of the same regimen or switch to capecitabine/oxaliplatin) for 3–6 months, tailored to response and tolerability.  
- 7. Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative FLR volume and liver volumetry results.  
- Baseline liver functional reserve (ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh score, MELD).  
- Detailed segmental location of each metastasis relative to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and hepatic artery branches.  
- Patient’s performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Prior exposure to chemotherapy (agents, duration, response).  
- KRAS/NRAS mutation status (for targeted therapy planning).  
- Exact timing and results of any prior postoperative imaging to confirm remission status.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

MDT Discussion: Late solitary metastasis, anatomically favorable for isolated resection.

Potentially resectable

- 3️⃣ Initiate systemic therapy: 6 cycles of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) ± bevacizumab given RAS wild‑type, aiming to treat occult micrometastases and potentially downsize lesions. Re‑assess CEA and imaging after chemotherapy.

- 5️⃣ Post‑operative care: monitor liver function, early mobilization, and initiate adjuvant chemotherapy (additional 6 cycles of FOLFOX) once recovery permits (usually within 6‑8 weeks).  
- 6️⃣ Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or CT every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative assessment of future liver remnant (volumetry).  
- Objective liver functional reserve (ICG‑R15, LiMAx, or comparable test).  
- Baseline performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary, renal).  
- History of prior systemic chemotherapy (type, cycles, hepatotoxicity).  
- Detailed hepatic parenchymal condition (steatosis, fibrosis, portal hypertension).  
These data are essential to confirm that a curative hepatectomy can be performed safely and to finalize the operative plan.

   • Obtain liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, albumin) and assess for portal hypertension.  
   • Perform volumetric CT or MRI to confirm that the future liver remnant will be ≥30 % of total liver volume.  
   • Review prior pathology to confirm R0 status of the primary rectal resection and ensure no residual disease.

   • Proceed to curative‑intent hepatic resection – preferably a laparoscopic or open segment VIII anatomical resection or non‑anatomical wedge excision, aiming for ≥1 cm negative margins.

   • KRAS mutation does not alter the choice of cytotoxic regimen; targeted agents are not indicated in the adjuvant setting for colorectal liver metastasis.  

4. Surveillance  
   • Follow NCCN/ESMO guidelines: contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest CT every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then every 6–12 months up to 5 years.  
   • Monitor CEA levels concurrently.

No critical information is lacking for a definitive recommendation; however, the following data would further solidify planning:  
• Detailed liver function panel (bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelet count) and assessment for portal hypertension.  
• Volumetric measurement of the future liver remnant.  
• Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (e.g., cardiovascular, pulmonary).

Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MRI shows four bilobar metastases (2‑3.5 cm) and volumetric analysis suggests that a curative‑intent hepatectomy may be possible, but adequacy of the future liver remnant (FLR) has not been confirmed. A prerequisite action—assessment of FLR with the option of portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy—is required before definitive surgery. Therefore the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.

- Verify baseline hepatic function (bilirubin, INR, albumin), performance status (ECOG), and comorbidities.  
- Obtain a detailed volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % with steatosis), plan PVE or a two‑stage hepatectomy.

- Aim for R0 resection with negative margins; intra‑operative ultrasound to locate all lesions.  
- Post‑operative: resume/adapt systemic therapy to complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy, considering oxaliplatin‑based regimen if not already completed.  
- Long‑term surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or CT every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
- Patient’s performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- KRAS/NRAS mutational status (relevant for anti‑EGFR therapy decisions).  
- Details of any prior adjuvant chemotherapy received after the initial colectomy.

Woman, 58 years old, left T4aN2M1 colon cancer with multiple bilobar metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + bevacizumab: 60% volumetric reduction, CEA dropped from 880 to 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: 5 remaining lesions, well-defined.
MDT Discussion: Major response to chemotherapy, surgical conversion considered.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient shows a substantial radiologic response (≈60% volume reduction) and a marked CEA decline, indicating chemosensitivity. However, definitive determination of hepatic resectability requires additional information that directly impacts feasibility: precise size and segmental location of each of the five residual lesions, their proximity to major vascular structures (hepatic veins, portal pedicles, inflow/outflow), and quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve. Without these data, it is unclear whether a single‑stage hepatectomy, a two‑stage approach, or portal vein embolization (PVE) will be necessary. Therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of these assessments.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy to complete a full conversion regimen (e.g., 12 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab or switch to FOLFIRI ± anti‑EGFR if RAS/BRAF wild‑type) while withholding bevacizumab at least 6 weeks before any planned operation.  
- Perform a comprehensive restaging work‑up within 2–3 weeks of the last chemotherapy dose: contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase, triphasic CT of chest/abdomen, and volumetric liver analysis (total liver volume, FLR calculation). Include liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and, if available, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin hepatobiliary scintigraphy.  
- If FLR ≥30 % (normal liver) or ≥40 % (post‑chemotherapy liver) and all lesions are amenable to clear margins without compromising major inflow/outflow, plan a simultaneous curative resection: left hemicolectomy (or completion colectomy if not yet performed) combined with an anatomic or non‑anatomic liver resection that clears all five lesions.  
- If FLR is insufficient or lesions are distributed such that a single‑stage resection would leave an inadequate remnant, adopt a staged hepatic strategy:  
   • Stage 1 – portal vein embolization of the liver sector to be resected (or ALPPS if rapid hypertrophy is required).  
   • Re‑assess FLR 2–4 weeks later; proceed to Stage 2 – definitive liver resection once adequate hypertrophy is confirmed.  
- Throughout the staged approach, maintain systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) between stages if disease control permits.  
- Post‑operative: resume adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 12–18 months of systemic therapy, tailored to pathologic response and molecular profile. Consider enrollment in a clinical trial for peri‑operative targeted therapy if appropriate.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact dimensions and segmental distribution of each hepatic lesion.  
- Relationship of lesions to hepatic veins, portal vein branches, and biliary ducts.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and functional assessment (ICG clearance or scintigraphy).  
- Current performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs. pending) and any residual disease on colonoscopy or imaging.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung nodules, peritoneal implants) on recent staging CT/PET.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide targeted therapy decisions.  
- Timing of the last bevacizumab dose relative to planned surgery.

• Resume systemic chemotherapy after recovery to complete a total of approximately 6 months of treatment (including preoperative cycles).

• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially very high tumor burden.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, sigmoid tumor with eight bilobar liver metastases. After 4 months FOLFIRI: radiological stability, CEA unchanged at 420 ng/mL. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases.
MDT Discussion: Stable disease, not resectable, discussion on continuing systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has eight bilobar colorectal liver metastases. Whether an R0 resection with an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver) can be achieved depends on the size, exact segmental location of each lesion, and the patient’s hepatic functional reserve. These decisive pieces of information are not provided. Consequently, a definitive “Resectable upfront” or “Not resectable” classification cannot be made; the case remains potentially resectable pending detailed hepatic volumetry, functional assessment, and multidisciplinary planning (e.g., two‑stage hepatectomy, portal vein embolization, or ALPPS).

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic chemotherapy with a conversion intent. Options include:  
  • Switch to a more intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) if tolerated, or add biologic agents based on molecular profile (anti‑EGFR for RAS‑wild type, bevacizumab for any RAS).  
- Obtain molecular profiling of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide targeted therapy.  
- After 2–3 additional cycles, repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging and perform volumetric analysis of the FLR.  
- If imaging shows sufficient tumor shrinkage or favorable distribution allowing a parenchymal‑sparing approach, plan a staged hepatic resection:  
  • Stage 1: Resection of lesions confined to one hepatic lobe or portal vein embolization of the future remnant lobe to induce hypertrophy.  
  • Interval (4–6 weeks) reassessment of FLR volume and tumor status.  
  • Stage 2: Completion hepatectomy or extended resection of remaining lesions, aiming for R0 margins while preserving ≥30 % functional liver.  
- For lesions that remain unresectable after maximal systemic therapy, consider percutaneous ablative techniques (RFA/MWA) or stereotactic body radiotherapy as adjuncts.  
- Management of the primary sigmoid tumor: if asymptomatic, defer resection until after hepatic clearance; otherwise, perform sigmoid colectomy (laparoscopic or open) either before or after liver surgery based on symptom burden and operative risk.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy should be administered according to standard colorectal cancer protocols, tailored to the response achieved and molecular findings.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed size and segmental location of each liver metastasis.  
- Quantitative liver volumetry (FLR percentage) and functional reserve (ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh, MELD).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities affecting surgical risk.  
- Molecular profile of the colorectal tumor (KRAS/NRAS/BRAF mutation status, MSI‑H/dMMR).  
- Baseline and trend of CEA beyond the single reported value (to assess biochemical response).  
- Prior response assessment according to RECIST criteria (percentage change in lesion diameters).  
- Presence of any other extra‑hepatic disease not captured on the reported thoracic CT (e.g., peritoneal implants, bone lesions).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases and, after 4 months of FOLFIRI, shows radiological stability with persistently elevated CEA (420 ng/mL). The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and absence of meaningful tumor downsizing make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable after major conversion.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Continuation and adaptation of systemic therapy
• Given the absence of radiologic response and stable high CEA, modification of the systemic regimen should be considered according to MDT discussion.
• The objective remains to achieve tumor downsizing sufficient to allow potential secondary resectability.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to detect any delayed response or change in lesion distribution.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant reduction in lesion size and number occurs, enabling parenchymal-sparing resections or multiples ablations or staged hepatectomy with adequate future liver remnant.

D. Alternative local strategies
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of all eight lesions on MRI.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case of potential future resection.
C. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation.
D. Status of the primary sigmoid tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for ongoing systemic therapy.
F. Complete extrahepatic staging to confirm disease confinement to the liver.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has shown a partial radiologic response to intensive chemotherapy with disappearance of three lesions and ≥40 % shrinkage of the remaining disease. However, definitive determination of hepatic resectability requires critical information that is not provided: precise anatomic distribution of the residual lesions, volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant, baseline liver function, and status of the rectal primary (local stage, response to therapy, need for radiotherapy). Because these data are essential to decide whether a single‑stage or staged hepatic resection is feasible, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the missing assessments.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI or switch to a regimen incorporating targeted agents based on molecular profile) for 2–3 additional cycles to maximize tumor shrinkage and allow time for further imaging.  
- Obtain high‑resolution, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences and 3‑D reconstruction to map all residual lesions, measure their size, and perform volumetric analysis of the future liver remnant.  
- Perform a thorough evaluation of the rectal primary: pelvic MRI and endorectal ultrasound to define T/N stage, assess mesorectal fascia involvement, and determine need for neoadjuvant chemoradiation.  
- If volumetry shows an insufficient FLR (<30 % in a normal liver, <40 % in a steatotic or chemotherapy‑injured liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
- Re‑stage the patient after imaging and functional assessment:  
   • If all residual lesions are confined to one hemi‑liver and an adequate FLR can be preserved, proceed to a single‑stage anatomical or non‑anatomical hepatic resection aiming for R0 margins.  
   • If lesions are bilobar and cannot be cleared safely in one operation, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in the future liver remnant, PVE, then second stage resection) or a simultaneous resection of the primary rectal tumor with limited hepatic resection if oncologically appropriate.  
- Following hepatic surgery, complete adjuvant systemic therapy (total 12 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy) and consider postoperative radiotherapy to the pelvis if indicated by the rectal pathology.  
- Throughout, monitor CEA trends and repeat imaging every 8–12 weeks to detect early progression.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact number, size, and segmental location of residual liver lesions after chemotherapy.  
- Volumetric data: total liver volume and calculated future liver remnant.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets) and presence of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Current staging and response of the rectal primary (MRI T/N stage, mesorectal fascia involvement, distance from anal verge).  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide targeted/immune therapy.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Details of prior or planned neoadjuvant radiotherapy for the rectal tumor.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. • Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

B. Precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.

F. a chest CT scan

Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, metastatic right colon cancer (KRAS mutated). After 8 cycles FOLFOX: progression of two lesions segment VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Progression on chemotherapy, no surgical window at this stage.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The two liver lesions (segments VII‑VIII, each up to 5.2 cm) are confined to a single hepatic lobe, which in principle could be addressed with a right hepatectomy if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) is present and the patient’s functional reserve is sufficient. However, critical information required to confirm surgical feasibility is missing (FLR volume, liver function, performance status, status of the primary colon tumor, and presence of any extra‑hepatic disease). Because these data are decisive for planning, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending their acquisition.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Switch to second‑line systemic therapy: FOLFIRI + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
- Re‑assess response after 2–3 cycles with contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI; aim for tumor shrinkage or disease stabilization.  
- If disease remains stable but FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the contralateral liver lobe.  
- For lesions that are borderline for resection or in case of limited response, evaluate locoregional options: hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC) or Y‑90 radio‑embolization to achieve down‑staging.  
- Once imaging confirms adequate FLR and disease control, plan a staged approach:  
   • First, resect the primary right‑sided colon cancer (if not already removed) – either laparoscopic right hemicolectomy or open, depending on tumor burden and patient condition.  
   • Second, after recovery (4–6 weeks), perform right hepatectomy with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance and negative margins.  
- If at any point extra‑hepatic progression appears or the patient’s performance status declines, shift to best supportive care or palliative systemic therapy.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Current performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, albumin) and presence of underlying liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis).  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant (CT‑based liver volumetry).  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected, unresected, symptomatic).  
- Evidence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) on recent imaging.  
- Comorbidities and cardiopulmonary reserve (cardiac ejection fraction, pulmonary function).  
- Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive versus palliative treatment.

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + panitumumab: complete disappearance of four foci and reduction of others at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA normalized.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response in several segments, uncertainty regarding microscopic persistence.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab the patient shows radiologic complete response of four hepatic lesions and partial response of the remaining lesions, indicating that disease burden has been markedly reduced.  
- Definitive determination of resectability requires precise information on the anatomic distribution of the residual metastases, their relationship to major vascular structures, and the anticipated future liver remnant (FLR).  
- Without volumetric data, liver function assessment, and confirmation that no extra‑hepatic disease is present, a safe surgical plan cannot be finalized; therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of these prerequisite evaluations.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- 1. Restaging work‑up: obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary agent (or gadoxetate‑enhanced MRI) and a PET‑CT to delineate residual hepatic disease, assess for occult extra‑hepatic metastases, and evaluate metabolic activity of the radiologically occult lesions.  
- 2. Functional assessment: perform liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin), indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin hepatobiliary scintigraphy, and calculate FLR volume using CT/MRI volumetry.  
- 3. Multidisciplinary review of imaging and functional data: if FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver (or ≥ 40 % after chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) and all lesions are amenable to an anatomic or non‑anatomic resection with negative margins, proceed to surgery.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (including possible ALPPS) to hypertrophy the future remnant.  
- 4. Surgical sequencing:  
   - a) If the primary left‑sided colon tumor has not yet been resected, schedule a combined approach (simultaneous colectomy and liver resection) when the extent of liver surgery is limited (≤ 3 segments).  
   - b) For extensive liver resection, perform staged surgery: first resect the primary tumor (laparoscopic or open left hemicolectomy), allow recovery, then proceed with hepatic resection after adequate FLR hypertrophy.  
- 5. Intra‑operative guidance: use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and achieve R0 margins; consider intra‑operative fluorescence imaging if indocyanine‑green is used pre‑operatively.  
- 6. Post‑operative management: resume systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR) for 3–6 months as adjuvant treatment, monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months, and consider enrolment in a clinical trial if available.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact segmental location and size of each residual hepatic lesion after chemotherapy.  
- Relationship of residual lesions to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume and liver function reserve (ICG clearance, bilirubin, INR, albumin).  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs. still in situ, distance from mesorectal margin).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants) on recent PET‑CT or high‑resolution CT.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Detailed molecular profile beyond RAS wild‑type (e.g., BRAF, MSI status) that may influence adjuvant therapy decisions.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab, four lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions have significantly decreased in size, with normalization of CEA. Despite this excellent response, the initial tumor burden and the phenomenon of “disappearing metastases” mean that viable microscopic disease may persist at the original sites. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but requires meticulous mapping of all initial metastatic locations before surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and systematically compare with pre-treatment imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy addressing initial disease map
• Plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided surgical approach that includes resection or ablation of all initial metastatic locations, not only residual visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to identify occult residual disease.
• Depending on lesion distribution, this may require a staged approach.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete surgical clearance of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the four “disappeared” metastases.
C. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of remaining lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
- Rationale: After 4 cycles of systemic therapy the number of liver lesions has decreased from ten to three and all are <2 cm, indicating a good tumor response. However, definitive resectability cannot be confirmed because critical information is lacking:  
  • Precise anatomic distribution of the three lesions (unilobar vs bilobar) and their relationship to major hepatic vessels or biliary structures.  
  • Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional reserve (e.g., ICG clearance, liver biochemistry).  
  • Status of the primary rectal tumor (resected, pending neoadjuvant chemoradiation, or still locally advanced).  
  • Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT, PET‑CT, peritoneal assessment).  
These missing data are decisive for planning a curative hepatectomy; therefore the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the above assessments.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy to deepen response and allow maximal tumor shrinkage:  
  • Maintain current regimen (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) and add targeted agent appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type disease (anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody) if not already included.  
  • Administer 2–3 additional cycles, monitoring CEA trend and tolerability.  
- Restaging after the additional cycles:  
  • Multiphasic liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging and volumetric analysis.  
  • Contrast‑enhanced chest CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
  • Endoscopic evaluation of the rectal primary; if still locally advanced, proceed with neoadjuvant chemoradiation (long‑course 5‑FU based) followed by reassessment.  
- Surgical planning based on restaging results:  
  • If lesions are confined to a single hepatic lobe and FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in steatotic liver), plan a single‑stage parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (segmental or wedge resections) aiming for R0 margins.  
  • If lesions are bilobar with insufficient FLR, consider a two‑stage approach: first stage portal vein embolization (PVE) of the lobe to be resected, followed by reassessment of FLR and second‑stage hepatectomy.  
  • Simultaneous resection of the rectal primary (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection) can be performed if the primary is resectable and patient’s performance status permits; otherwise schedule colorectal surgery after hepatic recovery.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: resume systemic chemotherapy (potentially with the same regimen) for 3–6 months, considering adjuvant anti‑EGFR therapy if indicated, and continue surveillance with serial CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact location of each hepatic lesion relative to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and liver function assessment (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT).  
- Current status of the rectal primary tumor (size, T stage after chemotherapy, need for chemoradiation, surgical plan).  
- Results of chest imaging and/or PET‑CT to exclude extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Detailed chemotherapy regimen used (agents, doses, anti‑VEGF/anti‑EGFR inclusion) and tolerance.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and baseline liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis).

Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases, CEA 600 ng/mL. On FOLFOX: overall stability, two new lesions detected at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Limited progression on treatment, question of changing protocol.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Classification: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases and newly identified extra‑hepatic lesions on thoraco‑abdominal CT, indicating disease progression despite FOLFOX. Surgical clearance would require (a) control of hepatic disease to achieve an adequate future liver remnant and (b) confirmation that the extra‑hepatic lesions are limited and amenable to resection or ablation. Both the response of the liver metastases to further systemic therapy and the resectability of the new thoracic lesions are currently unknown, making immediate surgery unsafe. Therefore the case meets the definition of “Potentially resectable” because a specific prerequisite – further systemic therapy with reassessment – must be completed before a definitive surgical plan can be made.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Switch systemic therapy to a more active regimen (e.g., FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX + bevacizumab) and incorporate targeted agents according to molecular profile (anti‑EGFR if RAS wild‑type, BRAF‑directed therapy if mutated, immunotherapy if MSI‑high).  
- Continue treatment for 2–3 months, monitoring tumor markers (CEA) and performing repeat high‑resolution thoraco‑abdominal CT or MRI to assess:  
   • Response of liver metastases (size reduction, number, distribution)  
   • Evolution of the new thoracic lesions (size, number, location)  
- If hepatic disease shows sufficient downsizing to allow a future liver remnant ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in steatotic liver) and the thoracic lesions are ≤3 cm, solitary or limited in number, and surgically accessible, proceed to a staged or simultaneous resection strategy:  
   • Consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if future liver remnant is marginal.  
   • Plan a liver‑first approach if hepatic disease is the dominant burden, followed by thoracic metastasectomy (video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery) after hepatic recovery.  
   • If both compartments can be safely addressed, a simultaneous colorectal primary resection, liver resection, and thoracic metastasectomy may be contemplated in a high‑volume center.  
- Throughout, maintain multidisciplinary oversight, including medical oncology, thoracic surgery, radiology, and hepatobiliary surgery, to adjust therapy based on response and toxicity.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Molecular profile of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status, HER2).  
- Detailed hepatic disease burden: number of lesions, maximal diameter of each, segmental distribution, and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Precise characteristics of the new thoracic lesions: size, number, laterality, relationship to major vessels/airways, and whether they are solitary pulmonary nodules or mediastinal/pleural disease.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and baseline liver function (bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelet count).  
- Current response to FOLFOX (RECIST measurements) and any treatment‑related toxicities.  
- Planned surgical margins required for colorectal primary (R0) and feasibility of achieving negative margins in the liver.  

These data are essential to finalize resectability determination and to tailor the optimal multimodal treatment plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases with the appearance of two new lesions while on FOLFOX, indicating disease progression under systemic therapy. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and ongoing progression make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The appearance of new lesions under FOLFOX indicates resistance to the current regimen.
• A change of systemic protocol is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± targeted therapy depending on molecular profile).
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of all liver lesions on MRI.
B. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
