Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has a single progressing hepatic lesion (5 cm in segment VII) after systemic chemotherapy, while the remaining lesions are stable or have disappeared. Surgical clearance would require control of the progressing lesion, either by down‑staging with additional systemic therapy or by local ablative treatment, before a definitive hepatectomy can be contemplated. The need for this prerequisite action (local control of the progressing metastasis) makes the case “Potentially resectable” rather than “Resectable upfront.”  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) for at least 2–3 cycles to maintain disease control and assess further response.  
- Apply a local ablative modality to the progressing segment VII lesion: percutaneous radiofrequency/ microwave ablation or stereotactic body radiotherapy, aiming for complete necrosis.  
- Re‑image (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) 4–6 weeks after local therapy to confirm response and to map the remaining stable lesions.  
- Perform volumetric liver assessment: calculate future liver remnant (FLR). If FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in the setting of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left liver.  
- Once adequate FLR is confirmed and all hepatic disease is controlled, plan a curative‑intent liver resection:  
   • If the stable lesions are confined to the left lobe, consider a left hepatectomy combined with wedge resections of any residual disease.  
   • If lesions are bilateral, consider a staged approach (right hepatectomy after PVE, followed by left‑sided resection) or a two‑step ALPPS procedure, depending on FLR and patient fitness.  
- Address the primary left‑colon tumor:  
   • If symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) – perform resection before or concurrently with liver surgery.  
   • If asymptomatic – consider simultaneous colon resection during the liver operation if operative time and physiologic reserve allow; otherwise, schedule colon resection after hepatic recovery.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy for at least 6 months, tailored to prior regimen and tolerability.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact anatomical distribution and size of the six stable hepatic lesions.  
- Relationship of lesions to major vascular structures (hepatic veins, portal pedicles).  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and presence of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
- Volumetric data to calculate future liver remnant.  
- Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Details of prior chemotherapy regimen, number of cycles, and timing of last dose.  
- Serum tumor markers (CEA) trend.  
These data are essential to confirm resectability, select the optimal surgical plan, and finalize the multidisciplinary treatment sequence.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial, residual, and disappeared lesions and detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
D. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Patient’s performance status for potential combined surgical/ablative strategy.
G. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The liver metastases are radiologically absent after 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, but imaging alone cannot exclude microscopic residual disease. Definitive surgical planning requires confirmation that the original sites are still amenable to resection with an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) and that the primary rectal tumor is resectable. Therefore a prerequisite step—high‑resolution liver MRI (with hepatocyte‑specific contrast) and possibly PET‑CT, plus assessment of liver function and FLR—must be completed before a definitive decision on liver surgery can be made.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- 1. Restaging work‑up: obtain liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted imaging, PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease, and calculate FLR using volumetric CT. Evaluate liver biochemistry, ICG clearance (if available), and performance status.  
- 2. Multidisciplinary review of restaging results:  
   • If imaging confirms no residual disease and FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % if liver steatosis or chemotherapy‑associated injury), proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery targeting the original metastatic zones (anatomic or non‑anatomic resection, or parenchymal‑sparing approach).  
   • If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to hypertrophy the remnant, followed by resection once adequate volume is achieved.  
- 3. Primary rectal tumor management:  
   • If the primary lesion has responded and is resectable, schedule low anterior resection (or appropriate sphincter‑preserving surgery) either synchronously with liver resection (if operative risk acceptable) or in a staged fashion after hepatic surgery.  
   • If the primary remains locally advanced, consider neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery before or after hepatic resection, based on multidisciplinary consensus.  
- 4. Post‑operative systemic therapy: administer adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 3–6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) after recovery, especially if high‑risk features (e.g., KRAS/NRAS mutation, poor differentiation) are present.  
- 5. Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact location, size, and number of the original liver metastases (to determine resection extent and FLR).  
- Baseline and current liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance).  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Detailed staging of the primary rectal tumor (T stage, nodal involvement, distance from anal verge, response to any neoadjuvant therapy).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung nodules, peritoneal implants).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and surgical risk assessment.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI status) that may influence adjuvant therapy decisions.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bilobar liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI, CT shows complete radiological disappearance of all lesions and CEA has normalized. Despite this apparent complete response, the high risk of occult residual microscopic disease at the sites of the initial metastases makes the situation potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely classifiable as disease-free without precise remapping of the original disease.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion-weighted sequences and compare meticulously with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, even if no lesion is currently visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

C. If surgical targeting of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

D. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the initial metastases relative to vascular structures.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and management plan of the rectal primary tumor : circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
E. Patient’s performance status for potential staged hepatectomy.
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer with bulky metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy: incomplete reduction, persistence of three lesions >5 cm. CEA 450 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Partial response insufficient, no criteria for immediate resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: Current imaging shows three hepatic lesions >5 cm after 8 cycles of systemic therapy, and the MDT has concluded that criteria for immediate resection are not met. Conversion to resectability will require either further tumor downsizing (additional chemotherapy/targeted agents) or clarification of key anatomic/functional parameters (future liver remnant volume, lesion proximity to major vessels, presence of extra‑hepatic disease). Because a specific prerequisite (further downstaging) and missing information are both present, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Verify molecular profile of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI, HER2) to select the most effective biologic agent for conversion therapy.  
- Continue systemic chemotherapy with a regimen proven to have high response rates in conversion settings (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with the appropriate targeted therapy based on molecular status.  
- Re‑image the liver after 2–3 additional cycles to assess tumor response and volumetric parameters.  
- If a sufficient radiologic response is achieved (≥30 % reduction in size) and volumetric analysis shows an adequate future liver remnant (≥30 % in a normal liver, ≥40 % if steatosis or chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is present), proceed to surgical planning.  
- Should the future liver remnant be marginal, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy before resection.  
- Plan a staged hepatic resection if lesions are bilobar or require extensive parenchymal sacrifice:  
   • Stage 1 – clearance of lesions in the future liver remnant (e.g., limited wedge resections or ablation).  
   • Stage 2 – major hepatectomy of the remaining diseased liver after hypertrophy is confirmed.  
- Simultaneously or sequentially address the primary colon tumor: if not yet resected, perform right hemicolectomy either before or after hepatic surgery, depending on patient’s performance status and intra‑operative considerations.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 12 cycles (or more) and consider maintenance biologic therapy if disease remains controlled.  
- Ongoing surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed liver imaging with volumetric assessment (future liver remnant calculation).  
- Precise anatomical location of each hepatic lesion relative to major vascular and biliary structures.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI status, HER2).  
- Current performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities affecting surgical risk.  
- Baseline liver function tests and assessment for chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
- Whether the primary colon tumor has already been resected or remains in situ.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bulky liver metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy, there is only partial reduction with persistence of three large lesions >5 cm and persistently elevated CEA (450 ng/mL). The residual tumor burden and limited response make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The insufficient response to current chemotherapy requires modification of the systemic regimen or consider intra arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary cancer, according to MDT decision.
• The objective remains to achieve further tumor downsizing that may open a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Given the high CEA level (450 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, reducing lesion size and allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains insufficiently responsive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the residual lesions on MRI.
B. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
C. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for further systemic therapy.
D. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
E. Previous systemic regimens received and tolerance.
F. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case a surgical window appears.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, operated two years earlier with a right hepatectomy for synchronous metastases from a left colon cancer. Surveillance: CEA 220 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two lesions segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Contralateral liver recurrence, anatomically accessible, no extra-hepatic disease.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: The two lesions are confined to segments II and III, which are anatomically accessible after a prior right hepatectomy. However, definitive determination of resectability requires (a) quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) after planned left‑lateral segmentectomy (segments II‑III) and (b) evaluation of hepatic functional reserve (e.g., ICG clearance, bilirubin, INR, albumin, presence of portal hypertension). Without these data, we cannot confirm that the remaining liver (primarily segment IV) will be sufficient to sustain postoperative liver function.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Obtain comprehensive hepatic functional work‑up and volumetric imaging (CT or MRI‑based liver volumetry) to calculate FLR.  
2. If FLR ≥ 30 % of total liver volume (or ≥ 40 % in the setting of prior chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) and liver function is adequate:  
   • Proceed with neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to treat occult micrometastatic disease and potentially downsize the lesions.  
   • Restage with repeat imaging and CEA; if disease remains confined to segments II‑III and FLR remains adequate, schedule left‑lateral segmentectomy (segments II‑III) with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance.  
   • Perform R0 resection; send margins for frozen section.  
   • Follow with adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen) for 3–6 months, tailored to response and tolerance.  
3. If FLR is insufficient (<30 % in a healthy liver, <40 % in a liver previously exposed to chemotherapy) but liver function is otherwise acceptable:  
   • Perform portal vein embolization (PVE) of the left lateral sector (segments II‑III) to induce hypertrophy of segment IV.  
   • Re‑assess FLR after 4–6 weeks; if adequate, repeat steps 2‑3 above.  
4. If FLR cannot be rendered adequate even after PVE or liver function is compromised:  
   • Consider locoregional ablative therapies (radiofrequency or microwave ablation) for the two lesions, combined with systemic chemotherapy.  
   • Reserve surgery for future if disease control is achieved and liver reserve improves.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative liver volumetry (total liver volume, FLR after planned resection).  
• Hepatic functional reserve assessments (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count, ICG clearance, presence/absence of portal hypertension).  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
• Details of prior peri‑operative chemotherapy (agents, cycles, liver toxicity).  
• Current imaging to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, PET‑CT if indicated).  
• Baseline nutritional status and frailty assessment.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two metachronous liver metastases in segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm) occurring in the left lateral section after a prior right hepatectomy, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesions are peripherally located but arise in the only remaining functional liver. Resection is technically feasible but must strictly preserve adequate parenchyma and inflow/outflow. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of previous major hepatectomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable with a strict parenchymal-sparing strategy, pending volumetric confirmation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative volumetric and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships and a chest CT scan.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (which is the current liver) and ensure preservation of sufficient functional parenchyma.
• Assess portal inflow and venous outflow carefully given prior right hepatectomy.

B. Peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (220 ng/mL) and early recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) may be considered.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability and adequate FLR are confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of the 2 lesions of segments II and III aiming for R0 margins.
• Avoid any formal left hepatectomy or extended resection.
• Depending on lesion distribution and FLR, this may be performed in a single stage or staged approach.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if given.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed vascular and biliary anatomy of segments II and III on MRI.
B. Exact volumetric assessment of the remaining liver (future liver remnant).
C. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Details of previous chemotherapy received before/after the first hepatectomy.
E. a chest CT scan F. Exact CEA trend prior to detection of recurrence.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of left R0 hepatectomy for liver metastases three years ago. CEA 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: single lesion segment VIII (3.8 cm) in contact with the IVC. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Deep solitary recurrence, technical assessment of resection required.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The solitary 3.8 cm lesion in segment VIII abuts the IVC, making the depth of vascular involvement a decisive factor that cannot be confirmed from the current report.  
- Confirmation of true IVC invasion versus mere contact, and an accurate volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) after a segment VIII resection, are required before a definitive surgical plan can be made.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Obtain high‑resolution, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI with dedicated vascular phases (or a dedicated IVC protocol) to delineate the extent of IVC involvement and to perform liver volumetry.  
- Perform baseline hepatic functional assessment (Child‑Pugh, MELD, ICG‑R15) and evaluate performance status/comorbidities.  
- If imaging confirms that the tumor does not infiltrate the IVC wall (contact only) and FLR is ≥30 % of total liver volume (or ≥40 % in a cirrhotic liver), proceed to a parenchymal‑sparing anatomic segment VIII resection with possible tangential IVC repair/patch; intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to confirm margins.  
- If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left liver remnant, followed by repeat volumetry after 4–6 weeks.  
- Given RAS‑wild‑type status, initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab; consider adding anti‑EGFR agent if the primary is left‑sided) for 2–3 months as neoadjuvant therapy to treat occult micrometastases and assess tumor biology. Re‑image after chemotherapy to confirm that the lesion remains resectable and that no new extra‑hepatic disease has appeared.  
- If restaging confirms resectability, proceed with the planned hepatic resection.  
- Post‑operative management: resume adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months of systemic therapy, and schedule regular CEA and imaging surveillance (every 3–6 months).  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Detailed vascular imaging to define IVC invasion depth.  
- Quantitative liver volumetry (FLR calculation).  
- Hepatic functional reserve (Child‑Pugh, MELD, ICG‑R15).  
- Performance status and comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary assessment).  
- Current status of the primary colorectal tumor (location, staging, prior treatment).  
- Full staging for extra‑hepatic disease (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, PET‑CT if indicated).  
- Prior systemic therapy regimens and response history.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver recurrence in segment VIII (3.8 cm) occurring after a prior left R0 hepatectomy. The lesion is deep and in contact with the IVC, in the only remaining right liver. Although solitary, the location adjacent to the IVC and the reduced liver reserve make resection technically demanding. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior major hepatectomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable, pending detailed vascular and volumetric assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform expert liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to precisely evaluate the relationship of the lesion to the IVC and right hepatic vein and a chest CT scan.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (which is the current liver) and assess inflow/outflow preservation.
• Evaluate whether R0 resection can be achieved without caval reconstruction.

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (180 ng/mL) and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status) may be considered to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing mandatory)
• If resectability is confirmed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if given.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed relationship of the segment VIII lesion to the IVC and hepatic veins on MRI.
B. Exact volumetric assessment of the remaining liver (future liver remnant).
C. chest CT scan.
D. Details of previous chemotherapy received before/after the first hepatectomy.
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
F. Exact CEA trend prior to detection of recurrence.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left hepatectomy performed two years prior. Liver MRI: three new lesions (segments V, VI, VII) measuring 1.5 to 2.8 cm.On the thoracic CT scan no other metastases. KRAS mutated, CEA 480 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Multiple liver recurrence, feasibility of local treatment to be re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
- The three hepatic lesions are confined to the right liver (segments V, VI, VII) and there is no extra‑hepatic disease on thoracic CT.  
- Because the patient has already undergone a left hepatectomy, the remaining liver is the right lobe; any further resection must leave an adequate future liver remnant (FLR).  
- Determination of whether a parenchymal‑sparing resection (segmentectomy or wedge) can achieve R0 margins while preserving ≥30 % FLR (≥40 % if liver function is impaired) requires volumetric imaging and functional liver assessment, which are not provided.  
- Therefore a specific prerequisite—pre‑operative FLR volumetry and liver function testing—is needed before a definitive surgical plan can be made, placing the case in the “Potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated colorectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI combined with bevacizumab).  
- Re‑evaluate after 2–3 months of therapy: obtain repeat liver MRI with volumetry, assess CEA trend, and perform liver function tests (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, INR).  
- If imaging shows stable disease or partial response and FLR is adequate, proceed to parenchymal‑sparing liver surgery:  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate lesion borders.  
   • Perform limited anatomical segmentectomy or non‑anatomical wedge resections of segments V, VI, and VII aiming for ≥1 cm margins.  
   • Preserve as much uninvolved right‑lobe parenchyma as possible.  
- If FLR is insufficient for safe resection, consider percutaneous or intra‑operative ablative modalities (radiofrequency or microwave ablation) for lesions ≤3 cm, either alone or combined with limited resection.  
- Post‑operative: resume systemic chemotherapy (same regimen) for 3–6 months; consider adding targeted therapy (e.g., anti‑VEGF) if not already used.  
- Continue surveillance with serial CEA, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI, and chest CT every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative liver volumetry (FLR percentage) after prior left hepatectomy.  
- Objective liver function assessment (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, INR, presence of portal hypertension).  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that could affect surgical risk.  
- Details of any prior systemic therapy (agents, duration, response).  
- Time interval between the previous hepatectomy and current recurrence.  
- Baseline pulmonary function if considering major hepatic resection.  
- Current CEA trend (baseline vs. current).

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The MRI shows multiple bilobar lesions up to 4.5 cm in a liver that has already undergone a left hepatectomy, making the future liver remnant (FLR) uncertain. Adequate FLR volume and functional reserve are decisive for any curative resection. Therefore, before a definitive surgical plan can be made, a quantitative FLR assessment (volumetry and functional testing) and, if necessary, portal vein embolization (PVE) or a staged hepatectomy must be performed. Until these data are obtained, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront,” nor can it be declared “Not resectable” because down‑staging and FLR augmentation may render a curative operation feasible.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Initiate systemic conversion chemotherapy: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (RAS wild‑type, high CEA suggests aggressive disease).  
2. Re‑evaluate after 2–3 months with contrast‑enhanced MRI and CEA trend.  
3. If radiologic response yields ≤4–5 lesions confined to one lobe or a reduction in tumor burden that would allow an FLR ≥30 % (≥40 % if underlying liver disease), proceed to step 4; otherwise continue systemic therapy or consider clinical trial/locoregional options.  
4. Perform detailed liver volumetry and functional assessment (ICG clearance, 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan).  
5. If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization of the future remnant side (right PVE if planning right‑sided resection, or left PVE if planning left‑sided completion hepatectomy).  
6. After hypertrophy (typically 2–4 weeks), repeat imaging; if disease remains resectable, undertake a curative‑intent hepatectomy—either a single extended resection if feasible, or a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS if bilobar disease persists but can be cleared sequentially.  
7. Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen) for 3–6 months, followed by surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3–4 months.  
8. If at any point disease progresses or extra‑hepatic metastases appear, shift to systemic therapy alone or palliative care as appropriate.

- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and functional reserve (ICG clearance, mebrofenin scan).  
- Detailed count and precise segmental location of each hepatic lesion relative to major vessels and biliary structures.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities affecting surgical risk.  
- Baseline liver biochemistry and any underlying liver disease (steatosis, fibrosis).  
- Prior systemic therapy received (agents, duration, response, toxicity).  
These data are essential to confirm whether a curative hepatectomy can be safely achieved after down‑staging.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, history of segmental VI-VII resection. Liver MRI: new lesion segment III (2.4 cm) and micronodule segment II. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous contralateral recurrence, possible minimally invasive approach depending on remnant volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The patient has a solitary 2.4 cm lesion in segment III and a micronodule in segment II after a prior segmental VI‑VII resection.  
- Parenchymal‑sparing resection (segmentectomy or wedge) is technically feasible, but the adequacy of the future liver remnant (FLR) cannot be confirmed without quantitative volumetry and functional assessment (e.g., ICG‑R15).  
- Because the decision hinges on a specific missing piece of information—precise FLR volume relative to the remaining liver after a left‑lateral resection—the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending that evaluation.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative work‑up  
  • Obtain contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI with volumetric analysis to calculate FLR; aim for >40 % FLR in a patient with prior hepatic resection.  
  • Perform liver function testing (bilirubin, albumin, INR) and ICG clearance to ensure adequate functional reserve.  
  • Review KRAS/NRAS status, CEA level, and complete staging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, PET‑CT if indicated) to exclude extra‑hepatic disease.  

- If FLR is adequate (≥40 %)  
  1. Proceed to minimally invasive (laparoscopic or robotic) left‑lateral resection – segmentectomy of segment III with wedge excision of the segment II micronodule, guided by intra‑operative ultrasound.  
  2. Aim for R0 margins (>1 cm when possible) while preserving as much non‑tumorous parenchyma as feasible.  
  3. Post‑operative recovery with early mobilization; discharge when liver function stable.  

- If FLR is insufficient  
  1. Consider right‑portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the left lobe, re‑assess FLR after 4–6 weeks.  
  2. Alternatively, if PVE is not desirable, treat the left‑lateral lesions with percutaneous ablation (RFA/MWA) as a bridge to surgery or as definitive local therapy.  

- Systemic therapy  
  • In the setting of metachronous recurrence, administer peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) either before (if FLR borderline) or after surgery, based on multidisciplinary consensus and patient tolerance.  
  • Continue adjuvant chemotherapy for a total of 6 months, adjusting regimen according to molecular profile (BRAF wild‑type, KRAS/NRAS status).  

- Surveillance  
  • Imaging (contrast MRI or CT) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months, combined with CEA monitoring.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative liver volumetry (FLR percentage) after planned left‑lateral resection.  
- Liver functional reserve assessment (ICG‑R15, bilirubin, albumin, INR).  
- KRAS/NRAS mutation status and baseline CEA level.  
- Details of any prior systemic therapy (agents, response, toxicity).  
- Comprehensive staging to rule out extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT/PET‑CT).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, operated two years earlier with a left hepatectomy.Liver MRI: recurrence segment VIII (3.1 cm) in contact with the middle hepatic vein. CEA 200 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Isolated complex recurrence of the hepatic dome, technical assessment required.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: The solitary 3.1 cm recurrence in segment VIII abuts the middle hepatic vein, and the patient has already undergone a left hepatectomy. Definitive resectability hinges on (a) quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) after a repeat right‑sided, segmental resection and (b) confirmation that hepatic venous outflow can be preserved or reconstructed. Without volumetric and functional liver reserve data, the operation cannot be scheduled outright.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Obtain a contrast‑enhanced CT volumetry (or MRI‑based volumetry) and liver function assessment (ICG‑15 clearance, bilirubin, platelet count, Child‑Pugh) to calculate FLR and ensure adequate hepatic reserve.  
2. Perform a multidisciplinary review of the vascular anatomy with 3‑D reconstruction to determine whether the middle hepatic vein can be spared, partially resected with patch reconstruction, or requires reconstruction using autologous or synthetic graft.  
3. If FLR is ≥30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver (or ≥40 % in a borderline liver) and venous outflow can be maintained, schedule a parenchymal‑sparing repeat hepatectomy: an anatomic segment VIII resection (or non‑anatomic wedge) with preservation of the middle hepatic vein when feasible; otherwise, resect the involved portion of the vein and reconstruct it. Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to delineate margins.  
4. If volumetry shows insufficient FLR, consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left remnant (which is already resected, so PVE would target the right posterior sector) or staged liver augmentation techniques (ALPPS) – though these are high‑risk after prior major hepatectomy and would be reserved for select cases.  
5. Regardless of the surgical plan, initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) now to control microscopic disease and to allow a short interval for liver assessment; stop bevacizumab ≥6 weeks before surgery to reduce bleeding risk.  
6. After resection, resume adjuvant systemic therapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) for at least 3–6 months, tailored to molecular profile (KRAS/BRAF, MSI status).  
7. Follow‑up with serial CEA, cross‑sectional imaging (CT/MRI) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative liver volumetry (FLR percentage) after planned repeat resection.  
- Functional liver reserve (ICG‑15, bilirubin, platelet count, Child‑Pugh, MELD).  
- Detailed vascular imaging (3‑D reconstruction) to define the extent of middle hepatic vein involvement and feasibility of preservation/reconstruction.  
- Performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary reserve).  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI) to guide systemic therapy.  
- History of prior systemic chemotherapy (agents, response, cumulative toxicity).  
- Evidence of extra‑hepatic disease (CT chest/abdomen, PET‑CT).  
- Current portal hypertension parameters (splenomegaly, varices).

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

MDT Discussion: Late isolated recurrence, anatomically approachable.

Resectable upfront  
- Single 3.9 cm metastasis confined to segment VII, no extra‑hepatic disease on imaging.  
- Prior bisegmentectomy IV‑V leaves segments I‑III, VI, VII, VIII; resection of segment VII alone will preserve an adequate future liver remnant (>30 % in a normal liver).  
- No vascular invasion described; lesion is anatomically approachable.  
- KRAS mutation does not affect technical resectability.

  • Obtain liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and calculate ICG clearance if available.  
  • Perform volumetric CT or MRI to confirm FLR >30 % (or >40 % if underlying liver disease).  
  • Review prior systemic therapy exposure and performance status (ECOG 0‑1 preferred).  
- Surgical plan  
  • Proceed to an anatomic segmentectomy of VII (or non‑anatomic wedge if intra‑operative ultrasound confirms clear margins).  
  • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate lesion borders and assess for additional occult disease.  
  • Aim for R0 resection with ≥1 cm margin when feasible.  
  • No need for portal vein embolization given expected adequate FLR.  
- Post‑operative oncologic management  
  • Pathology review for margin status, tumor regression grade, and molecular profile (KRAS confirmed).  
  • Initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (6 months) – preferred regimen FOLFOX ± bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease still benefits from anti‑VEGF).  
  • Consider enrollment in a clinical trial if available (e.g., adjuvant immunotherapy for microsatellite‑stable disease).  
- Surveillance  
  • CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
  • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for 3 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
No essential data are lacking to make a reliable resectability assessment or to outline a definitive management plan. Essential information such as liver function, volumetry, performance status, and prior systemic therapy should be confirmed but is not currently a barrier to proceeding with the recommended approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 72 years old, right hepatectomy 4 years ago. Current liver MRI: multiple nodules segment III, 1-2 cm. CEA 550 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Multifocal recurrence, assessment of resectability and local alternatives.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The lesions are confined to segment III, but the patient has already undergone a right hepatectomy, leaving a limited left‑liver remnant.  
- Definitive determination of feasibility requires quantitative liver volumetry and functional assessment (e.g., Child‑Pugh, ICG clearance) to ensure an adequate future liver remnant after any additional resection or ablation.  
- Absence of this information makes it impossible to declare the case “Resectable upfront,” while there is no oncological or anatomical contraindication that would render it “Not resectable.”  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- 1️⃣ Baseline evaluation: obtain full liver function panel, Child‑Pugh score, ICG‑R15, and perform CT‑ or MRI‑based volumetry of the remaining left liver (segments II‑IV).  
- 2️⃣ Multimodal planning:  
   • If volumetry shows a future liver remnant ≥30‑35 % (adjusted upward for age >70 y), proceed with a parenchymal‑sparing approach – either a limited segment III wedge resection or percutaneous/ intra‑operative microwave ablation, preserving segment II.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization of the left portal branch to hypertrophy segment II, or a staged approach (e.g., ALPPS) only after careful risk‑benefit discussion given the patient’s age.  
- 3️⃣ Systemic therapy: because the tumor is RAS wild‑type and CEA is markedly elevated, initiate neoadjuvant chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) for 2–3 months. This may downsize microscopic disease, treat occult extra‑hepatic micrometastases, and provide a biologic response assessment.  
- 4️⃣ Restaging: repeat contrast‑enhanced MRI (or PET‑CT) after systemic therapy to reassess lesion size, number, and any new extra‑hepatic sites.  
- 5️⃣ Decision point:  
   • If disease remains limited to segment III and FLR criteria are met, schedule curative‑intent surgery/ablation.  
   • If new extra‑hepatic disease appears or lesions progress, shift to systemic therapy alone or consider palliative local therapies.  
- 6️⃣ Post‑operative follow‑up: serial CEA monitoring and imaging every 3‑4 months for the first two years, with consideration of adjuvant chemotherapy if not given pre‑operatively.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Current liver function status (Child‑Pugh, MELD, bilirubin, albumin, platelets).  
- Quantitative liver volumetry of the left liver (segments II‑IV) and calculation of future liver remnant after planned resection.  
- Exact number and spatial relationship of the segment III nodules to major vessels/ducts.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, etc.) on recent staging scans.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that could affect surgical risk.  
- Details of any prior adjuvant or neoadjuvant therapy after the original right hepatectomy.

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer with three liver metastases (2-4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 620 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Synchronous hepato-pulmonary involvement, discussion of sequential strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The three hepatic lesions (2‑4 cm) are within size limits for hepatic resection, but the adequacy of future liver remnant (FLR) has not been documented.  
- Bilateral pulmonary nodules represent extra‑hepatic disease; their resectability cannot be confirmed without detailed thoracic imaging and pulmonary functional assessment.  
- Current oncologic practice for synchronous colorectal liver and lung metastases recommends systemic chemotherapy first to assess tumor biology and to potentially downsize lesions before committing to major surgery. Therefore a prerequisite systemic therapy and complete thoraco‑abdominal evaluation are required before definitive resection can be planned.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated disease (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 3–6 months, monitoring CEA trend and radiologic response.  
- Perform restaging contrast‑enhanced CT (or MRI for liver) after chemotherapy to evaluate:  
   • Size and number of hepatic lesions, FLR volume, need for portal vein embolization (PVE) if FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in steatotic liver).  
   • Morphology and resectability of pulmonary nodules; obtain PET‑CT if not already done to exclude additional metastatic sites.  
- If imaging shows adequate FLR and pulmonary lesions are amenable to resection, proceed with a staged surgical plan:  
   1. First stage – hepatic resection (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing depending on lesion location) performed either alone or simultaneous with primary colon resection if oncologically safe.  
   2. Recovery interval of 4–6 weeks, then pulmonary metastasectomy (video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery or open, based on nodule location).  
- If FLR is insufficient, schedule PVE (or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS) before hepatic resection.  
- After completion of all resections, administer adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (same regimen or modified) for an additional 3–6 months, guided by postoperative CEA and pathology.  
- Throughout treatment, maintain multidisciplinary surveillance with repeat imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative liver volumetry (future liver remnant percentage).  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, ICG clearance).  
- Detailed thoracic imaging (exact location of pulmonary nodules, relationship to vessels/bronchi).  
- Pulmonary function tests (FEV1, DLCO) to confirm surgical fitness.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities.  
- Any prior systemic therapy or response data.  
- Molecular profile beyond KRAS (e.g., BRAF, MSI status) that could influence systemic options.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases (2–4 cm) and two bilateral pulmonary nodules in the setting of a left T4N2 colon cancer, without other reported sites. The presence of limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lungs) does not preclude a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be cleared. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease appears technically resectable. Category: Potentially resectable

- Initiate systemic induction chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab or FOLFOX + bevacizumab) for 2–3 months; obtain baseline molecular profile (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H) to guide targeted agents.

- Baseline liver function tests and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Exact distribution and burden of peritoneal disease (PCI score or operative findings).

- Initiate systemic therapy: 3–6 months of intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS wild‑type status.  
- Re‑stage after chemotherapy: contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or CT, chest CT, and calculate FLR using volumetric software.  
- If imaging shows sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % in steatotic liver), proceed to curative surgery:  
   • Option A – Simultaneous liver and lung resection (single operative session) if patient’s cardiopulmonary reserve permits and operative time is acceptable.  
   • Option B – Staged approach: first liver resection (potentially two‑stage hepatectomy or portal vein embolization if FLR borderline), followed by pulmonary metastasectomy after recovery (typically 4–6 weeks later).  
- If FLR is insufficient after chemotherapy, consider portal vein embolization or ALPPS to augment liver remnant before definitive hepatectomy.  
- For any residual liver lesions unsuitable for resection, apply percutaneous ablation (RFA/MWA) intra‑operatively or as a bridge.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6–12 months of systemic therapy, adjusted based on pathologic response and postoperative recovery.

- Baseline performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiovascular, pulmonary, hepatic).

Man, 62 years old, left colon cancer with six liver metastases and lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 780 ng/mL.

Response:

Potentially resectable  
- Six hepatic metastases may be cleared surgically, but feasibility depends on their segmental distribution, size, relationship to major vascular structures, and the volume of future liver remnant (FLR).  
- The hepatic‑pedicle lymph node represents extra‑hepatic disease; resection is possible only if the node can be safely removed and there is no further distant spread.  
- At present the case lacks critical anatomic and functional data (detailed liver imaging, FLR calculation, liver function, performance status) that are decisive for confirming upfront resection. Therefore the lesions are considered potentially resectable pending further evaluation and/or down‑staging therapy.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated left‑sided colorectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) with the goal of tumor shrinkage and assessment of disease biology.  
- After 2–3 months, restage with high‑resolution liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted and hepatobiliary‑specific sequences) and CT‑based volumetry to define:  
   • Number, size, and segmental location of each metastasis  
   • Proximity to portal/hepatic veins and bile ducts  
   • Calculated FLR (target >30 % in normal liver, >40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected)  
- If imaging shows sufficient downsizing and an adequate FLR, proceed to a combined operative plan:  
   1. Left hemicolectomy (or primary tumor resection) with oncologic lymphadenectomy.

- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen) for 3–6 months, adjusted based on pathological response and postoperative recovery.  
- If restaging demonstrates progression, extensive vascular involvement, or inadequate FLR, shift to a non‑curative approach: continue systemic therapy, consider targeted agents, and provide best supportive care.

- Precise anatomic details of each liver metastasis (size, segment, proximity to major vessels/ducts).  
- Quantitative assessment of future liver remnant volume and baseline liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelets).  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Confirmation that the hepatic‑pedicle node is the only extra‑hepatic site (absence of distant nodal or organ metastases).  
- Results of a high‑quality liver MRI or contrast‑enhanced CT with volumetry.  
- Baseline cardiopulmonary evaluation to ensure tolerance of major abdominal surgery.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Not resectable: The presence of eight bilobar hepatic metastases together with moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis indicates that a curative‑intent hepatectomy is not feasible. Bilobar disease would require an unacceptably small future liver remnant, and peritoneal spread represents extra‑hepatic disease that precludes a liver‑only resection. No combination of limited resections can achieve R0 margins while preserving adequate liver function.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy with an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) unless contraindicated by comorbidities or performance status.  
- Obtain baseline molecular profiling (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR) to guide targeted or immunotherapy options.  
- Re‑image after 2–3 months of therapy to assess radiologic response of both liver and peritoneal disease.  
- If a marked response yields ≤3 liver lesions confined to one lobe and peritoneal disease regresses to a low peritoneal cancer index (PCI ≤ 5), consider conversion to a staged approach:  
   • First, resect the primary colon tumor (right hemicolectomy) to prevent obstruction or bleeding.  
   • Second, evaluate candidacy for major hepatectomy with portal vein embolization or ALPPS if future liver remnant remains insufficient.  
   • Third, if peritoneal disease becomes limited, discuss cytoreductive surgery with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC).  
- If disease remains extensive after systemic therapy, continue palliative chemotherapy, consider liver‑directed therapies (Y‑90 radioembolization, hepatic arterial infusion) for symptom control, and provide best supportive care.  
- Throughout, monitor CEA trends and maintain multidisciplinary review at each decision point.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Patient’s ECOG performance status / ASA classification.  
- Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine green clearance or similar assessment of hepatic reserve.  
- Quantitative assessment of peritoneal disease (PCI score) and exact distribution.  
- Volumetric analysis of future liver remnant.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS/NRAS/BRAF status, MSI‑H/dMMR).  
- Details on comorbidities that may limit chemotherapy or surgical options.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases associated with moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (970 ng/mL). The presence of peritoneal dissemination combined with extensive bilobar hepatic disease excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (970 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of liver lesions.
C. Molecular profile to optimize systemic treatment.
D. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
E. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.
F. Patient’s performance status for staged surgical procedures.

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, five bilobar liver metastases (1.5-3.5 cm). CEA 1150 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.Liver MRI: contact of segment VIII lesion with middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable disease, high tumor marker suggests systemic risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: The liver metastases are technically resectable, but optimal oncologic management requires a prerequisite systemic chemotherapy phase to (a) assess tumor biology given the markedly elevated CEA and multiple bilobar lesions, and (b) potentially downsize disease and improve margin status, especially for the segment VIII lesion abutting the middle hepatic vein. Until this neoadjuvant treatment and its response are documented, definitive resection cannot be scheduled.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate peri‑operative systemic therapy: 2–3 months of a fluoropyrimidine‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) or triplet (FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab, recognizing KRAS mutation excludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
- Re‑stage after chemotherapy: repeat contrast‑enhanced MRI/CT of the liver, assess CEA trend, and calculate future liver remnant (FLR). If FLR is <30 % in a normal liver, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the remnant.  
- Surgical plan based on response:  
   • If disease remains resectable with adequate FLR, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection. A two‑stage or “reverse” approach (liver first) can be used given the bilobar distribution; simultaneous colon resection is acceptable if the primary is uncomplicated and the patient’s physiologic reserve permits.  
   • For the segment VIII lesion in contact with the middle hepatic vein, plan a parenchymal‑sparing resection with possible wedge resection of the vein or reconstruction, depending on intra‑operative assessment.  
- Post‑operative management: complete a total of 6 months of systemic therapy (including the pre‑operative cycles) as adjuvant treatment, with surveillance CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years.  
- If progression occurs during neoadjuvant therapy, shift to a palliative systemic regimen and reassess for any further local‑ablative options.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities affecting surgical risk.  
- Baseline liver function tests and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung, peritoneum) on staging CT/PET.  
- Detailed anatomic relationship of all lesions to major vascular structures beyond the middle hepatic vein (portal branches, hepatic arteries).  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (obstruction, perforation) and whether it has been resected or requires urgent surgery.  
- Laboratory parameters relevant to chemotherapy tolerance (renal function, neutrophil count, etc.).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases (1.5–3.5 cm), including a segment VIII lesion in contact with the middle hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. From a technical standpoint, complete clearance with parenchymal-sparing resections appears feasible while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is potentially resectable. However, the very high CEA level (1150 ng/mL) suggests aggressive tumor biology and a high systemic risk.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 5 lesions to segment VIII vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy
• The elevated CEA level (1150 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Give 3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Surgical management (staged strategy)
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first multiple atypical resection for the 5 lesions and/or segmentectomy 8 with en-bloc partial resection a the middle hepatic veine removing the 5 metastases, or a formal right hepatectomy if anatomically more appropriate, and if volume of the remnant liver is sufficient, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin .
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Precise segmental distribution of the three lesions within the left liver and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
C. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
D. a chest CT scan

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven liver metastases (2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 1600 ng/mL. BRAF V600E mutation, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, poor prognosis linked to molecular profile.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- Seven hepatic lesions ranging 2‑5 cm are likely bilateral; achieving an R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver) cannot be confirmed without volumetric data.  
- No information is provided on lesion proximity to major vascular or biliary structures, which could preclude parenchymal‑sparing resections.  
- Because the critical missing information (precise anatomical distribution and quantitative FLR assessment) directly determines whether a curative hepatectomy is feasible, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending further evaluation (e.g., liver volumetry, possible portal vein embolization).  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic therapy aimed at tumor down‑staging and addressing the aggressive BRAF‑mutated biology:  
  • First‑line: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (or FOLFOX/FOLFIRI + bevacizumab if tolerability is a concern).  
  • Consider enrollment in a clinical trial incorporating a BRAF inhibitor (encorafenib) plus anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) ± MEK inhibitor if available.  
- Re‑image the liver after 2–3 cycles (≈8 weeks) to assess radiologic response and re‑evaluate resectability.  
- If sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % after chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) are confirmed:  
  • Plan a staged hepatectomy strategy:  
    – Perform portal vein embolization (PVE) of the lobe to be resected if FLR is borderline.  
    – Re‑assess FLR 2–3 weeks post‑PVE; proceed to curative liver resection (anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing) once adequate hypertrophy is achieved.  
  • Simultaneously or sequentially address the primary colon tumor:  
    – If the primary is asymptomatic, consider delayed right hemicolectomy after liver surgery to minimize peri‑operative risk.  
    – If symptomatic (obstruction/bleeding), perform right hemicolectomy first, followed by systemic therapy and liver‑directed treatment.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy: continue the same regimen or switch to a BRAF‑targeted combination (encorafenib + cetuximab) for at least 6 months, depending on intra‑operative findings and pathology.  
- Throughout treatment, monitor CEA trends and perform surveillance imaging every 8–12 weeks to detect early progression.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Detailed hepatic imaging with volumetric analysis (CT‑based or MRI‑based liver volume, FLR calculation).  
- Exact anatomical distribution of each metastasis (unilobar vs bilobar, relation to portal/hepatic veins, biliary ducts).  
- Baseline liver function tests and functional reserve assessment (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, platelet count).  
- Patient performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that may affect surgical tolerance.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) on full staging work‑up.  
- KRAS/NRAS status (though BRAF V600E is known, concurrent RAS mutation influences anti‑EGFR use).  
- Prior treatments, if any, and patient preferences regarding aggressive multimodal therapy.

• Any surgical consideration would remain highly selective.

• Continue systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, T3N2 upper rectal cancer with four liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 980 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases with MSI-H profile opening discussion for first-line immunotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has four bilobar liver metastases and a locally advanced upper rectal primary (T3N2). Although the number of lesions does not automatically preclude resection, definitive resectability depends on (a) achieving an adequate future liver remnant after hepatic clearance and (b) controlling the primary rectal tumor. Because the disease is MSI‑high, first‑line checkpoint‑inhibitor therapy is indicated and may downsize hepatic lesions, but response must be documented before a surgical plan can be finalized. Therefore a prerequisite systemic (immunotherapy) and possibly neoadjuvant rectal treatment are required prior to definitive resection.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate first‑line immunotherapy (e.g., pembrolizumab or nivolumab ± ipilimumab) given MSI‑H status and metastatic burden.  
- Simultaneously evaluate the rectal primary: if symptomatic or at high risk for local progression, deliver neoadjuvant radiotherapy (short‑course 5 × 5 Gy or long‑course chemoradiation) according to multidisciplinary consensus.  
- After 8–12 weeks of systemic therapy (and completion of radiotherapy if given), restage with high‑resolution liver MRI and pelvic MRI or endorectal ultrasound. Assess:  
   • Size and number of hepatic lesions, distribution relative to vascular inflow/outflow, and calculate future liver remnant (volumetry, indocyanine‑green clearance if needed).  
   • Response of the rectal primary (down‑staging) and nodal status.  
- If hepatic disease shows partial response or stable disease and an adequate FLR (>30 % in normal liver, >40 % if steatosis/fibrosis), plan curative‑intent liver surgery:  
   • Consider a staged approach (e.g., right‑sided resection first, portal vein embolization to hypertrophy left lobe, then left‑sided resection) or a simultaneous hepatectomy with total mesorectal excision (TME) if operative risk acceptable and FLR sufficient.  
- Perform TME (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection as dictated by tumor location and response) either concurrently with liver resection or in a second operation after hepatic clearance, based on intra‑operative assessment and patient fitness.  
- Post‑operative management: resume immunotherapy for a total of at least 2 years or until disease progression, and consider adjuvant chemotherapy if pathological high‑risk features persist.  
- Enroll patient in surveillance program with serial CEA, cross‑sectional imaging, and colonoscopic follow‑up.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact size and segmental location of each liver metastasis.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelet count) and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Details of rectal tumor assessment (MRI staging, distance from anal verge, involvement of mesorectal fascia).

- Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive multimodality therapy.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

Woman, 70 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, two liver metastases segments II and III (3.2 and 4.0 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 320 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type, HER2 positive.
MDT Discussion: Limited involvement but HER2 mutation may influence systemic therapeutic strategy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectable upfront  
The two hepatic lesions are confined to segments II and III, are ≤5 cm, and are anatomically amenable to a left‑lateral sectionectomy with an adequate future liver remnant (right liver). No vascular invasion or extra‑hepatic disease is reported. The primary colon tumor is resectable (left‑sided T3N1).   • Cardiopulmonary assessment and performance‑status (ECOG 0‑1).  
- Surgical plan (simultaneous resection):  
  1. Standard oncologic left‑sided colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy.  
  2. Left‑lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) with negative margins (R0).

  • 6 months of oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy (CAPOX or FOLFOX).

  • Consider KRAS/NRAS testing if not already done to confirm eligibility for anti‑EGFR agents (though HER2‑targeted regimen is preferred).  
- Surveillance:  
  • CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
  • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.
